title: A Single Intra-articular Injection of Autologous Stromal Vascular Fraction for Moderate-to-Severe Knee Osteoarthritis: Results of a Multicenter Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial With 12-Month Follow-up.
authors: Garza JR, Moorman CT 3rd, Baria M, Santa Maria D, Bowen J, Sparks N, Rubin JP
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov 5:3635465261498163. doi: 10.1177/03635465261498163. 
Online ahead of print.

A Single Intra-articular Injection of Autologous Stromal Vascular Fraction for 
Moderate-to-Severe Knee Osteoarthritis: Results of a Multicenter Randomized 
Placebo-Controlled Trial With 12-Month Follow-up.

Garza JR(1), Moorman CT 3rd(2), Baria M(3), Santa Maria D(4), Bowen J(5), Sparks 
N(6), Rubin JP(7).



BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial evaluated the 12-month outcomes of 
a single intra-articular injection of autologous adipose-derived stromal 
vascular fraction (SVF), prepared and administered during the same clinical 
encounter, for the treatment of moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis (OA).
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: To evaluate the efficacy of a single intra-articular 
injection of 25 million autologous adipose-derived SVF cells for 
moderate-to-severe knee OA, compared with placebo, at 12 months. The authors 
hypothesized that SVF-treated patients would demonstrate a significantly greater 
responder rate based on prespecified clinically meaningful improvements in pain 
and function derived from composite outcomes of the index and contralateral 
knees.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1.
METHODS: Adults aged 35 to 85 years with symptomatic unilateral or bilateral 
knee OA were eligible if the index knee demonstrated a Western Ontario and 
McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index pain score of ≥8, an Outerbridge 
grade of 2 to 4 on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and a Kellgren-Lawrence 
grade of 2 to 4 on radiographs. Autologous adipose-derived SVF was prepared 
using a point-of-care isolation system during the same clinical encounter, 
assessed against predefined release criteria, and administered as a single 
intra-articular injection into the index knee. MRI of the index knee was 
obtained at baseline and at 12 months.
RESULTS: A total of 618 participants were assessed for eligibility, of whom 114 
were randomized (SVF, n = 83; placebo, n = 31). At 12 months, a single 
intra-articular injection of 25 million SVF cells demonstrated statistical 
superiority over placebo for the primary composite clinical endpoint. The 
responder rate was 51.8% (43/83) in the SVF group compared with 29% (9/31) in 
the placebo group (difference, 22.8% [95% CI, 3.5%-42%]; 1-sided P = .0149). No 
serious investigational device-related adverse events were reported.
CONCLUSION: A single intra-articular injection of 25 million autologous 
adipose-derived SVF cells resulted in statistically superior and clinically 
meaningful improvements in pain and function at 12 months compared with placebo, 
with no serious investigational device-related adverse events reported.
REGISTRATION: IDE 16734; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04440189.

PMID: 42989897

title: Technology Assistance and Fixed-Bearing Design Were Associated with Higher Revision-Free Survival at 15 Years After UKA: A Cohort Study of 2,234 Consecutive Knees.
authors: Tsukamoto I, MacInnis BR, Grimm JA, Bedard NA, Sierra RJ, Pagnano MW, Abdel MP, Hannon CP
abstract:
1. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2026 Nov 5. doi: 10.2106/JBJS.26.00507. Online ahead of 
print.

Technology Assistance and Fixed-Bearing Design Were Associated with Higher 
Revision-Free Survival at 15 Years After UKA: A Cohort Study of 2,234 
Consecutive Knees.

Tsukamoto I(1), MacInnis BR, Grimm JA, Bedard NA, Sierra RJ, Pagnano MW, Abdel 
MP, Hannon CP.



BACKGROUND: Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) is an alternative to total 
knee arthroplasty for isolated compartment osteoarthritis; however, concerns 
persist regarding its long-term durability. The purpose of this study was to 
evaluate revision-free survivorship, risk factors for revision, and clinical 
outcomes in a large consecutive series of contemporary UKAs.
METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive primary UKAs performed from 
2000 to 2021 at a single tertiary academic center. Revision-free survivorship 
was estimated using a Kaplan-Meier analysis, and risk factors for revision were 
assessed using Cox proportional hazards modeling. Clinical outcomes were 
assessed using the Knee Society Score (KSS).
RESULTS: A total of 2,234 UKAs were included. Fixed-bearing implants were used 
in 78% of UKAs. Technology assistance was used in 59% of UKAs (fluoroscopy, 43%; 
robotic assistance, 15%; computer navigation, 1%). The mean patient age was 65 
years, the mean body mass index was 31 kg/m2, and 49% of UKAs were performed in 
female patients. Patient race was White in 97% of UKAs, and patient ethnicity 
was not Hispanic or Latino in 94%. Revision-free survivorship was 92% at 10 
years and 85% at 15 years. Overall, 118 UKAs were revised, most commonly through 
conversion to total knee arthroplasty (97%). The most frequent indications for 
revision were progression of osteoarthritis in an adjacent compartment (41%), 
aseptic loosening (23%), unexplained pain (9%), and hardware failure (9%). 
Factors associated with a lower risk of revision in the univariable analysis 
included technology assistance (hazard ratio [HR], 0.4; p < 0.01) and high 
surgeon volume (HR, 0.5; p < 0.01). Mobile-bearing design (HR, 1.9; p < 0.01) 
was associated with an increased risk of revision in the univariable analysis. 
The mean KSS improved from 47 preoperatively to 75 at 5 years postoperatively (p 
< 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In this large consecutive series, UKA demonstrated excellent 
long-term survivorship, with an approximately 1% annual risk of revision through 
15 years. Technology assistance, a fixed-bearing implant design, and high 
surgeon volume were each associated with a lower risk of revision, underscoring 
the importance of operative technique and implant selection in achieving durable 
outcomes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a 
complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Increased risk of infection and reoperation following total knee arthroplasty in patients under 40.
authors: Daley A, Yarden J, Diaz-Coto S, Moschetti W
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Nov 2;64:104663. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104663. Online ahead of 
print.

Increased risk of infection and reoperation following total knee arthroplasty in 
patients under 40.

Daley A(1), Yarden J(2), Diaz-Coto S(2), Moschetti W(2).



BACKGROUND: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is increasingly performed in younger 
patient populations. This study aimed to compare perioperative outcomes between 
patients under 40 and those over 65, stratified by surgical indication.
METHODS: This retrospective study used the Epic Cosmos dataset to identify 
primary TKA patients under 40 years old (n = 3,177) or over 65 (n = 698,662). 
Patients were stratified by surgical indication (primary osteoarthritis, 
post-traumatic osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, avascular necrosis, and 
multiple indications) using ICD-10 codes. Outcomes included superficial wound 
dehiscence, infection, readmission, and ipsilateral reoperation, assessed at 
90 days and 1 year postoperatively. Differences between age groups were assessed 
using adjusted odds ratios (95% confidence intervals) derived from multivariable 
logistic regression models adjusted for sex, body mass index, comorbidity 
burden, insurance status and smoking status with significance set at p < 0.05. A 
sensitivity analysis in the overall cohort tested the interaction between age 
group and surgical indication.
RESULTS: Surgical indications differed significantly between cohorts 
(standardized proportions difference 0.939, p < 0.001), with osteoarthritis 
accounting for 97.8% of cases in patients >65 compared to 64.6% in patients <40. 
Younger patients had higher rates of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (2.4% vs 
0.1%) and multiple diagnoses (20.7% vs 1.6%). Among patients with 
osteoarthritis, those under 40 had significantly higher 90-day odds of infection 
(OR 3.16, 95% CI 2.29-4.35), superficial wound dehiscence (OR 1.91, 95% CI 
1.34-2.72) and ipsilateral reoperation (OR 3.91, 95% CI 3.34-4.58), which 
persisted at 1 year (infection OR 2.79, 95% CI 2.13-3.67; superficial wound 
dehiscence OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.41-2.59; reoperation OR 3.44, 95% CI 3.00-3.94). 
Patients under 40 with multiple diagnoses had elevated odds of infection at 
90 days (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.15-3.69) and 1 year (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.09-2.95), and 
ipsilateral reoperation at 90 days (OR 3.10, 95% CI 2.25-4.25) and 1 year (OR 
2.71, 95% CI 2.06-3.55). In the overall cohort, the effect of age differed 
significantly by surgical indication for all outcomes except superficial wound 
dehiscence.
CONCLUSION: Patients under 40 undergoing Total Knee Arthroplasty are at 
increased risk for prosthetic joint infection, superficial wound problems and 
ipsilateral reoperation at 90 days and 1 year when compared to those over the 
age of 65, independent of smoking status and comorbidity burden. Those with 
multiple indications for surgery are also at increased risk for infection and 
same-side reoperation at both time points.

title: Formal consensus on fast-track hip and knee arthroplasty: ESSKA/EKA, EHS and APAS recommendations for optimised recovery pathways in joint replacement surgeries.
authors: Totlis T, Kort N, Kort R, Budhiparama NC, Carulli C, Clarius M, Coden G, Gamie Z, Gomberg B, Grant A, Guenther D, Haddad FS, Kayani B, Kenanidis E, Królikowska A, Liu D, Lumban-Gaol I, Machado L, Nandi S, Pérez-Prieto D, Prill R, Smith E, Tandogan R, Tsiridis E, Beek RV
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4239-4255. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70594. Epub 2026 Sep 16.

Formal consensus on fast-track hip and knee arthroplasty: ESSKA/EKA, EHS and 
APAS recommendations for optimised recovery pathways in joint replacement 
surgeries.

Totlis T(1)(2), Kort N(3), Kort R(3), Budhiparama NC(4)(5)(6), Carulli C(7), 
Clarius M(8), Coden G(9), Gamie Z(10)(11), Gomberg B(12), Grant A(9)(13), 
Guenther D(14), Haddad FS(15)(16), Kayani B(17), Kenanidis E(10)(11), 
Królikowska A(18), Liu D(19), Lumban-Gaol I(6)(20), Machado L(21)(22), Nandi 
S(23), Pérez-Prieto D(24)(25), Prill R(26), Smith E(9)(27), Tandogan R(28), 
Tsiridis E(10)(11), Beek RV(29).



PURPOSE: This international formal consensus aims to establish a unified, 
evidence-based approach to perioperative care by promoting the adoption of 
fast-track surgery or enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocols, 
informing healthcare professionals and administrators about optimal 
perioperative management of arthroplasty and facilitating broader 
implementation.
METHODS: A multidisciplinary panel of 106 experts contributed across a Steering 
Group (n = 22), a Rating Group (n = 35) and a Peer Review group (n = 49). The 
Steering Group developed 37 questions and corresponding statements based on the 
literature review and expert opinion. Statements were graded from A (high-level 
evidence) to D (expert opinion). An independent Rating Group evaluated each 
statement on a 1-9 Likert scale across two rounds using the Formal Consensus 
methodology. Statements were iteratively revised and finalised through consensus 
and joint discussion. The final document was assessed by an international Peer 
Review Group to ensure transnational applicability.
RESULTS: Out of 37 questions, a total of 63 statements were developed. Following 
a set of general statements outlining the principles and overall goals of 
fast-track total knee arthroplasty (TKA) and total hip arthroplasty (THA), the 
recommendations addressed and optimised the three key phases of perioperative 
care: preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative management. Of the 63 
statements, 39 were graded A or B and 24 as C or D. Mean agreement scores ranged 
from 7.7 to 8.9. Overall, 56 statements were considered appropriate with strong 
agreement and 7 with relative agreement. The Peer Review Group supported the 
overall statements, providing feedback to clarify specific recommendations and 
to highlight regional differences in implementation, which were incorporated 
into the final document.
CONCLUSIONS: This consensus endorses the adoption of structured fast-track or 
enhanced recovery programs as a patient-centred approach to perioperative care 
in total hip and knee arthroplasty. The aim is to improve the quality of care by 
reducing morbidity, optimising pain management, shortening hospital stay and 
enhancing patient satisfaction. While not intended to replace clinical 
judgement, it provides a pragmatic framework to guide decision-making, promote 
consistency and facilitate safe early mobilisation and discharge.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.

title: Implant-Related Complications After Robotic-Assisted Versus Manual Revision Knee Arthroplasty: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.
authors: Mzeihem M, Rteil A, Farid Y, Martini O, Piponov H, Puri L, Amirouche F
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3133-e3143. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01589. Epub 2026 Jul 31.

Implant-Related Complications After Robotic-Assisted Versus Manual Revision Knee 
Arthroplasty: A Propensity-Matched Cohort Study.

Mzeihem M(1), Rteil A, Farid Y, Martini O, Piponov H, Puri L, Amirouche F.



INTRODUCTION: As robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA) gains traction 
in revision procedures, the urgent need to investigate its effectiveness 
compared with manual methods becomes apparent.
METHODS: Data were retrospectively obtained from the TriNetX Collaborative 
Network. Revision TKA (rKA) cases were identified using CPT codes and 
categorized as manual or robotic assisted using ICD-10 procedure codes. Cohorts 
were balanced with 1:1 propensity score matching for demographics, 
comorbidities, and revision history. Complication rates were compared across 
follow-up using chi-square analysis.
RESULTS: An initial query identified 19,088 manual and 2,709 robotic-assisted 
rKA cases. After 1:1 propensity matching, 2,010 patients remained in each group. 
Robotic rKA had significantly lower mechanical implant‑related complications at 
3 and 6 months (OR 1.67 and 1.66; P < 0.001) and lower early VTE, while PJI, 
readmission, and revision rates were not significantly different. Manual rKA 
showed higher opioid use at 0 to 3 months (OR 1.40, 95% CI, 1.14 to 1.71, P < 
0.001) and 3 to 6 months (OR 1.28, 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.47, P < 0.001) and 
throughout the 3 years of follow-up.Throughout the follow-up period, patellar 
dislocation, wound infection, non‑implant-related complications, and transfusion 
did not differ. At 1 year, manual rKA had higher instability (OR 1.59; P = 
0.001) and higher hazard of mechanical implant‑related complications (HR 1.52, 
95% CI, 1.32 to 1.75; P = 0.049). Instability, loosening, and periprosthetic 
fracture remained higher at 2 to 3 years, and revision was significantly more 
frequent at 3 years (13.5% vs. 11.4%; OR 1.22, 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.46; P = 0.03).
DISCUSSION: Robotic-assisted rKA was associated with markedly lower mechanical 
implant‑related complications across early and midterm follow-up, including 
reduced rates of instability, aseptic loosening, periprosthetic fracture, VTE, 
and lower opioid requirements. Rates of PJI, readmission, and revision were 
largely comparable, although manual rKA demonstrated a markedly higher revision 
rate by 3 years. These findings suggest that robotic assistance may improve 
implant reliability and postoperative recovery, but prospective studies and 
cost-effectiveness analyses remain necessary.

title: Preresection hyperextension is associated with greater initial extension laxity and site-specific reductions in bone resection without substantial joint-line lowering in robot-assisted cruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Morita Y, Shin J, El-Hassan M, Shichman I, Lewis S, Dundon JM, Long WJ, Sculco PK
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 6. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70680.
Online  ahead of print.

Preresection hyperextension is associated with greater initial extension laxity 
and site-specific reductions in bone resection without substantial joint-line 
lowering in robot-assisted cruciate-retaining total knee arthroplasty.

Morita Y(1), Shin J(1), El-Hassan M(1), Shichman I(1), Lewis S(2), Dundon 
JM(2)(3), Long WJ(1), Sculco PK(1).



PURPOSE: Associations of preresection hyperextension with intraoperative laxity, 
bone resections, joint-line height and clinical outcomes were examined in 
cruciate-retaining (CR) robot-assisted total knee arthroplasty (TKA).
METHODS: In this retrospective single-surgeon cohort, knees were classified by 
initial intraoperative extension angle as control (0° to +5°), mild 
hyperextension (-5° to <0°) or greater hyperextension (<-5°). Intraoperative 
balance, surgical adjustments, joint-line height, 6-week clinical extension and 
1-year Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement 
(KOOS-JR) outcomes were evaluated. Adjusted associations were assessed using 
regression models.
RESULTS: Among 258 knees (149 control, 76 mild and 33 greater), greater initial 
extension laxity was observed in both hyperextension groups versus controls, 
with adjusted differences of 1.1° (95% CI, 0.4-1.9) and 2.4° (1.1-3.7), 
respectively. Postoperative hip-knee-ankle angle differences versus controls 
(n = 256) were 0.1° (95% CI, -0.9 to 1.0) and -0.6° (-1.8 to 0.7), respectively. 
Among 109 hyperextension knees, each 5° greater hyperextension was associated 
with smaller distal lateral femoral and proximal medial tibial resections 
(adjusted β, -1.0 mm [95% CI, -1.6 to -0.3] and -1.2 mm [-1.7 to -0.6]; 
false-discovery-rate-adjusted p = 0.016 and p < 0.001). Mean joint-line lowering 
was 0.3 mm (95% CI, 0.02-0.60), without a significant association with 
hyperextension magnitude. No significant differences were detected in final 
extension imbalance or 6-week extension. Paired KOOS-JR scores were available 
for 208 knees, without significant group differences in scores or improvement. 
Greater hyperextension was associated with higher adjusted odds of patient 
acceptable symptom state (PASS) failure versus combined control and 
mild-hyperextension groups (OR, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.02-7.08; p = 0.045).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater preresection hyperextension was associated with greater 
initial extension laxity, smaller selected resections and higher adjusted odds 
of PASS failure. Minimal average joint-line change was observed. Using initial 
sagittal assessment to individualise resection planning is supported.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

title: Greater eccentric hamstrings to concentric quadriceps strength ratio at 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with reduced odds of revision within 2 years.
authors: Högberg J, Cristiani R, Samuelsson K, Mikkelsen C, Hamrin Senorski E
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 6. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70679.
Online  ahead of print.

Greater eccentric hamstrings to concentric quadriceps strength ratio at 6 months 
after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with reduced odds 
of revision within 2 years.

Högberg J(1)(2), Cristiani R(3)(4), Samuelsson K(1)(5)(6), Mikkelsen C(3)(4), 
Hamrin Senorski E(1)(2).



PURPOSE: To investigate the association between eccentric 
hamstrings-to-concentric quadriceps strength ratio (mixed hamstrings to 
quadriceps [HQ]-strength ratio) at 6 months postoperatively and revision 
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACL-R) within 2 years of primary 
surgery. The secondary purpose was to investigate the association between the 
mixed HQ-strength ratio and single-leg hop for distance limb symmetry index 
(LSI).
METHODS: Data were collected from a local registry at Capio Artro Clinic, 
Stockholm, Sweden. Patients aged ≥15 years, without concomitant ligament 
injuries and meniscal resection or repair who underwent primary ACL-R with 
hamstring tendon autografts between 2005 and 2021 were included. Isokinetic 
eccentric hamstrings and concentric quadriceps strength were assessed using a 
Biodex dynamometer 6 months postoperatively. Associations between mixed 
HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg and revision ACL-R were analysed using 
multivariable logistic regression analysis, presented with odds ratios (ORs), 
95% confidence intervals (CIs) and area under the receiver operating 
characteristics curve (AUC). Associations between mixed HQ-strength ratio and 
single-leg hop for distance LSI were analysed with linear regression.
RESULTS: Of the 3458 patients included, 49.5% were female and the mean age was 
28.8 ± 10.4 years. Patients who underwent revision ACL-R within 2 years had 
lower mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg 6 months postoperatively. After 
adjustment for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level, each 10-unit 
increase in the mixed HQ-strength ratio on the ACL-R leg was associated with 
lower odds of revision ACL-R (OR = 0.81, 95% CI [0.71;0.93], p = 0.003). 
However, the discriminatory ability was poor (AUC = 0.64). A greater mixed 
HQ-strength ratio was associated with poorer single-leg hop for distance LSI, 
adjusted for age at primary ACL-R and preinjury Tegner level (β = -1.30, 95% CI 
[-1.51;-1.09], p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: The mixed HQ-strength ratio may complement the evaluation of muscle 
strength recovery after ACL-R. However, its poor discriminatory ability limits 
its use to identify patients who will undergo revision ACL-R.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.
authors: Davies PSE, Banziger C, Lawless AM, O'Brien SS, Ebert JR, Edwards PK, Tahir M, Ranjit S, Mcewan JK, Malik SS, D'Alessandro PA
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70671.
Online  ahead of print.

Gracilis tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction impairs gracilis muscle volume 
recovery and may adversely affect adjacent thigh musculature. MRI-based outcomes 
from a subgroup of patients enroled in the DOSTAR randomized controlled trial.

Davies PSE(1)(2), Banziger C(3), Lawless AM(1), O'Brien SS(1), Ebert 
JR(2)(4)(5), Edwards PK(2), Tahir M(6), Ranjit S(1)(2), Mcewan JK(2)(7), Malik 
SS(8)(9), D'Alessandro PA(1)(2)(10).



PURPOSE: Segmentation of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows accurate 
calculation of muscle volumes. The Dual Or Single Tendon Anterior cruciate 
ligament Reconstruction (DOSTAR) study is a prospective randomized controlled 
trial investigating a semitendinosus (ST) graft with adjustable button tibial 
fixation versus a dual tendon semitendinosus and gracilis (STG) graft with screw 
tibial fixation in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The purpose 
of the present study is to investigate differences in thigh muscle volume at 6 
and 12 months between these treatment groups.
METHODS: Patients were randomized and underwent ACLR using either a ST or STG 
graft construct. MRI of bilateral thighs was completed at 6 and 12 months 
post-operatively. Muscle volumes were measured in both thighs at both time 
points in both groups.
RESULTS: A total of 38 patients underwent MRI scanning at 6 and 12 months. There 
was a significant difference in the interval volume change of gracilis in the 
STG group compared to the ST group (-1.6 cm3 ± 4.6 vs. +2.8 cm3 ± 6.8, 
p = 0.026). Interval gracilis hypertrophy occurred in 35% (7/20) of cases in the 
STG group and 67% of cases (12/18) in the ST group (p = 0.103). Adductor longus 
(AddL) also demonstrated a significant difference in interval volume change 
between the STG and ST group (-2.4 cm3 ± 12.0 vs. +11.1 cm3 ± 21.2, p = 0.020). 
AddL hypertrophy occurred in 30% of cases (6/20) in the STG group and 72% 
(13/18) in the ST group (p = 0.022). All other muscles had no significant 
differences noted in muscle recovery between groups. Linear regression analysis 
demonstrated a significant positive relationship between interval changes in 
gracilis and AddL volumes (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: The present study provides MRI evidence that gracilis tendon 
harvest was associated with persistent impairment of gracilis muscle recovery 
and may also adversely affect AddL. This adds to the growing body of evidence 
supporting the use of ST with adjustable button graft constructs for hamstring 
ACLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, subgroup analysis of prospective, double-blinded, 
randomized controlled trial.

title: Individualised total knee arthroplasty results in low reintervention rates for stiffness and instability in 1000 consecutive knees, regardless of intraoperative bone recuts or polyethylene thickness.
authors: Schmidt A, Sappey-Marinier E, Alajji M, Ferrini A, Aït-Si-Selmi T, Bonnin M
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70670.
Online  ahead of print.

Individualised total knee arthroplasty results in low reintervention rates for 
stiffness and instability in 1000 consecutive knees, regardless of 
intraoperative bone recuts or polyethylene thickness.

Schmidt A(1), Sappey-Marinier E(1), Alajji M(1), Ferrini A(1), Aït-Si-Selmi 
T(1), Bonnin M(1).



PURPOSE: Individualised total knee arthroplasty (TKA) aims to restore the 
pre-arthritic anatomy, but concerns persist regarding ligament imbalance, as 
only two polyethylene insert thicknesses are available. This study aimed to 
evaluate revision and reintervention rates, especially for stiffness and 
instability, after individualised TKA, and whether intraoperative adjustments 
influenced these outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included 1000 consecutive primary TKAs 
implanted using a CT-based individualised system with a 1-year minimum 
follow-up. The primary endpoint was any revision TKA. Secondary analyses 
evaluated reintervention for stiffness or instability and the association 
between reinterventions and (1) bone recuts and (2) polyethylene thickness. 
Survival was estimated with the Kaplan-Meier method.
RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 4.2 ± 1.8 years, 12 revision TKA (1.2%) and 29

BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes after platelet-rich plasma (PRP) treatment for 
knee osteoarthritis are inconsistent, and some well-designed trials show no 
benefit. Whether a standardized multicomponent pathway improves outcomes 
relative to conventional PRP care is uncertain.
PURPOSE: To compare the efficacy, safety, satisfaction, and costs of a 
standardized PRP pathway versus physician-directed conventional PRP care in 
Kellgren-Lawrence grade I and II knee osteoarthritis.
STUDY DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1.
METHODS: At 3 hospitals, 240 patients were randomized 1:1 to a standardized PRP 
clinical pathway (PRP-CP; n = 120) or physician-directed conventional PRP care 
(PRP-C; n = 120). PRP-CP combined standardized selection, quality-controlled 
leukocyte-poor PRP, ultrasound-guided injections, staged rehabilitation, and 
systematic follow-up. Primary 12-month outcomes were visual analog scale (VAS) 
pain, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) 
total, and International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) scores; secondary 
outcomes included achievement of the minimal clinically important difference, 
satisfaction, adverse events, and costs.
RESULTS: At 12 months, PRP-CP produced greater changes than PRP-C in VAS (mean 
difference [MD], -2.98 [95% CI, -3.64 to -2.32]), WOMAC total (MD, -8.63 [95% 
CI, -11.35 to -5.90]), and IKDC (MD, 10.25 [95% CI, 8.37 to 12.13]) scores (all 
P < .001). Achievement of the minimal clinically important difference favored 
PRP-CP at 3, 6, and 12 months for the VAS and at 6 and 12 months for the IKDC 
and WOMAC (P < .05). Satisfaction was greater with PRP-CP (odds ratio, 1.79 [95% 
CI, 1.11-2.89]; P = .017). An adverse event occurred in 17 of 115 patients in 
the PRP-CP group (14.8%) versus 36 of 113 patients in the PRP-C group (31.9%) 
(Fisher exact test: P = .003). Mean costs were CN¥15,199.9 versus CN¥14,754.4, 
respectively; the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was CN¥66.0 per WOMAC 
point. Effects were generally consistent across centers, and blinding was 
maintained.
CONCLUSION: The standardized multicomponent pathway produced greater 12-month 
improvements in pain and function than conventional PRP care, with fewer adverse 
events. Because components were bundled and no placebo group was included, the 
trial does not establish PRP efficacy or component-specific effects.

BACKGROUND: For patients with open physes approaching skeletal maturity, 
transphyseal anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) with soft tissue 
autograft and metaphyseal fixation is often preferred. Although iatrogenic 
physeal injury is rare, growth disturbances have been reported. This study 
sought to evaluate postoperative changes in lower extremity alignment 1 year 
after transphyseal ACLR in skeletally immature patients within 2 years of 
skeletal maturity.
HYPOTHESIS: Transphyseal ACLR would not result in clinically significant changes 
in alignment.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 2.
METHODS: This was a prospective multicenter study of skeletally immature 
patients with ≤2 years of remaining growth who underwent primary transphyseal 
soft tissue autograft ACLR. The change in the difference in alignment parameters 
between involved and uninvolved extremities from preoperative assessment to 1 
year postoperative was calculated (difference of differences = Δ2) to account 
for naturally occurring alignment changes during growth. Radiographic 
measurements included mechanical axis deviation (MAD), anatomic lateral distal 
femoral angle (aLDFA), mechanical medial proximal tibial angle (mMPTA), 
posterior tibial slope (PTS), and leg length discrepancy (LLD).
RESULTS: A total of 91 patients (48 males) merited inclusion with a median 
skeletal age of 14.0 years. Reconstructions were performed with hamstring (46%) 
or quadriceps (54%) autograft. The cohort-wide median Δ2 values for MAD (2.9 
mm), aLDFA (-1°), mMPTA (0°), and LLD (0.1 cm) were small. However, 28% of 
patients demonstrated a ≥10-mm Δ2 in MAD (73% into valgus), and Δ2 for aLDFA and 
mMPTA was ≥5° in 17% (73% into valgus) and 16% (43% into varus) of patients, 
respectively. One patient (1%) subsequently was recommended for intervention for 
growth disturbance at latest follow-up.
CONCLUSION: This study of skeletally immature individuals with ≤22 years of 
growth remaining who underwent transphyseal ACLR with soft tissue autograft and 
metaphyseal fixation demonstrated minimal cohort-wide changes in alignment at 1 
year postoperatively. However, a meaningful subset of patients (16%-28%) 
demonstrated clinically relevant changes in alignment, most commonly into valgus 
and decreased tibial slope. These findings warrant routine preoperative 
radiographic assessment and surveillance until skeletal maturity. Further study 
is needed to define thresholds for implant-mediated guided growth in patients 
with borderline valgus preoperatively who may be at risk of progressive 
deformity.

title: Can Psychological Readiness Predict Successful Return to Sports After Patellar Stabilization Surgery in Adolescent Patients? A Retrospective Cohort Study.

abstract:

Epub  2026 Oct 9.

Can Psychological Readiness Predict Successful Return to Sports After Patellar 
Stabilization Surgery in Adolescent Patients? A Retrospective Cohort Study.

Kim CL(1), Turlip RW(2), Thothadri M(1), Redler LH(3), Greenberg E(1), Williams 
BA(1)(2).



BACKGROUND: While many metrics are used to subjectively assess a patient's knee 
function with patellofemoral instability (PFI), psychological readiness to 
return to sport (RTS) after patellar stabilization surgery is not well 
established in this population. The Anterior Cruciate Ligament Return to Sport 
After Injury (ACL-RSI) scale assesses psychological readiness to RTS after 
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and may be similarly beneficial in 
understanding this domain in those with PFI.
HYPOTHESIS: Higher ACL-RSI scores in patients with PFI are associated with an 
increased likelihood of RTS after patellar stabilization surgery.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of adolescent patients (10-19 
years old) treated surgically for PFI (medial patellofemoral ligament 
reconstruction [MPFLR] with or without tibial tubercle osteotomy) at a single 
institution from January 2020 to October 2024. Patients actively participating 
in sports at their first orthopaedic visit who completed the ACL-RSI during 
postoperative rehabilitation were included. Patient demographics, injury 
characteristics, surgical procedure, ACL-RSI scores, and RTS status were 
recorded. Descriptive statistics and bivariate analysis were performed. Based on 
the euclidean distance, the optimal ACL-RSI cutoff score for predicting 
successful RTS was determined, and diagnostic accuracy was evaluated with a 
receiver operating curve. A multivariate logistic regression, adjusted for sex, 
was used to identify predictors of RTS.
RESULTS: Study criteria identified 97 patients with a median (IQR) age of 15.6 
years (14.2-16.4). Seventy underwent isolated MPFLR and 27 underwent MPFLR with 
tibial tubercle osteotomy. Successful RTS was achieved in 78.3% (n = 76). RTS 
was associated with higher ACL-RSI scores (P = .012), isolated MPFLR (P = .011), 
and male sex (P = .03). An ACL-RSI score ≥59.2 was identified as being 
indicative of successful RTS (area under the curve, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.56-0.83). 
While procedure type and ACL-RSI scores were both associated with RTS in 
univariate analysis, the multivariable analysis adjusting for sex revealed that 
the ACL-RSI cutoff remained the only significant predictor of RTS (odds ratio, 
3.56; 95% CI, 1.10-11.51; P = .033).
CONCLUSION: ACL-RSI scores ≥59.2 are associated with an increased likelihood of 
successful RTS after surgical treatment for PFI in adolescents. Patient 
demographics and the studied injury characteristics do not appear to influence 
the likelihood of successful RTS.

BACKGROUND: The limb symmetry index (LSI) is a measure comparing strength and 
functional movement between the surgical and nonsurgical limbs, used after 
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) to guide rehabilitation and 
assess return-to-sport readiness. With increasing use of the quadriceps tendon 
autograft (QT-ACLR), limited data exist on whether the LSI score correlates with 
patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs).
HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: To evaluate the predictive value of postoperative strength 
and functional LSI tests at 3, 6, and 9 months for short-term PROMs, determine 
Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) thresholds, and assess differences based 
on PASS achievement. It was hypothesized that quadriceps strength LSI score 
would more strongly predict 2-year PROMs than hamstring strength LSI score, and 
that higher 9-month isokinetic quadriceps LSI scores would be associated with 
higher International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) and Lysholm scores.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: Patients undergoing primary QT-ACLR from 2021 to 2024 with LSI testing 
during rehabilitation (isometric and isokinetic lower extremity strength, 
Y-Balance, hop testing) and no revision or additional knee surgery were 
included. The LSI score was assessed at 3, 6, and 9 months, and PROMs, including 
Lysholm and IKDC scores, were collected at a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years. 
Multivariable linear regression was used to evaluate associations between LSI 
measures and PROMs after adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). 
Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to determine PASS 
thresholds.
RESULTS: A total of 100 knees in 100 patients (mean age, 25.3 ± 11.2 years; BMI, 
25.9 ± 6.5 kg/m2; 52% male) were included. Quadriceps and hamstring strength and 
functional performance progressively improved from 3 to 9 months, with the LSI 
score reaching 77% to 81% for quadriceps strength and 98% to 100% for hamstring 
strength by 9 months postoperatively. At a mean follow-up of 2.0 ± 0.7 years, 
the mean satisfaction score was 8.4 of 10, the Lysholm score was 90.7, and the 
IKDC score was 77.8. Linear regression, adjusted for age, sex, and BMI, 
demonstrated that 3-month isometric quadriceps LSI score had a strong effect on 
IKDC score, explaining substantial variance (β = 3.9; adjusted R2 [AdjR2] = 
0.36; P < .03); 6-month isokinetic quadriceps and hamstrings showed moderate but 
significant effects (β = 2.9-3.7; AdjR2 = 0.13-0.17; P < .05) on IKDC score; and 
9-month fast quadriceps had a strong effect explaining substantial variance in 
Lysholm and IKDC scores (β = 3.9-4.7; AdjR2 = 0.34-0.35; P ≤ .003). Lysholm and 
IKDC scores correlated with satisfaction and accurately discriminated PASS 
thresholds (area under the curve, 0.927-0.937; P < .001). Patients achieving the 
IKDC PASS demonstrated higher LSI scores across time points and all PROMs.
CONCLUSION: After QT-ACLR, strength-associated LSIs were independently 
associated with PROMs at a mean 2-year follow-up, after adjusting for age, sex, 
and BMI. Early isometric quadriceps strength at 3 months predicted higher 2-year 
IKDC scores, with PASS achievers generally attaining a 60% to 70% LSI score by 3 
months. Isokinetic quadriceps strength at 9 months predicted both IKDC and 
Lysholm scores. These findings highlight the importance of early quadriceps 
strength recovery and the value of LSI measures in predicting PROMs and 
informing early rehabilitation.

title: Age-Dependent Variations in Knee Synovial Fluid Biomarker Type and Concentration Predict 5- to 10-Year Outcomes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
authors: Ehlers M, Kurtz JL, Montgomery SR Jr, Kaplan DJ, Strauss EJ
abstract:

Age-Dependent Variations in Knee Synovial Fluid Biomarker Type and Concentration 
Predict 5- to 10-Year Outcomes After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.

BACKGROUND: Synovial fluid biomarkers reflect the intra-articular response to an 
anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture and may provide insight into biological 
processes associated with posttraumatic joint degeneration. While increasing age 
has been associated with inferior clinical outcomes after ACL reconstruction, 
age-dependent differences in biomarker expression and their relationship to 
longer term outcomes remain unclear.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the association 
between patient age and preoperative synovial biomarker concentrations after an 
ACL injury to determine whether age modifies biomarker-outcome relationships at 
longer term follow-up. The authors hypothesized that increasing age would be 
associated with an elevated inflammatory response and modify biomarker-outcome 
associations.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: Patients undergoing ACL reconstruction between July 2011 and December 
2020 were prospectively enrolled. Synovial fluid was aspirated before incision, 
and concentrations of proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory biomarkers were 
quantified. Patients completed patient-reported outcome (PRO) measures, 
including the visual analog scale for pain, Lysholm scale, Tegner Activity 
Scale, and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score-Physical Function Short 
Form, at a minimum of 5 years postoperatively. Multivariable regression assessed 
associations between age and biomarker concentrations. Conditional process 
analysis evaluated moderation by symptom duration and mediation by cartilage 
injury severity. Associations between age and long-term PROs were assessed using 
multivariable regression and minimal clinically important difference analyses.
RESULTS: A total of 100 patients were included (mean age, 30.8 ± 9.5 years). 
Increasing age was independently associated with lower preoperative synovial 
TIMP-1 concentrations (β = -0.0775; P = .014). This association was moderated by 
symptom duration, with significant effects at <3.0 and >8.5 months. Cartilage 
injury severity did not mediate age-biomarker associations. Increasing age was 
associated with worse long-term PROs and the decreased likelihood of achieving 
the minimal clinically important difference for pain, function, and activity. 
After adjusting for age, higher MIP-1β concentrations were associated with worse 
functional outcomes, higher MMP-3 concentrations were associated with greater 
pain, higher TIMP-2 concentrations were associated with lower activity levels, 
and higher bFGF concentrations were associated with improved physical function. 
Significant age-dependent interactions were observed for TIMP-1, TIMP-2, and 
MIP-1β with selected PROs. Age-stratified analysis demonstrated heterogeneous 
biomarker-outcome associations.
CONCLUSION: Patient age at the time of ACL reconstruction was associated with 
selective alterations in synovial biomarker expression and long-term clinical 
outcomes. Age modified the prognostic significance of key biomarkers, 
highlighting the importance of incorporating age into biomarker interpretation 
and risk stratification after an ACL injury.

PURPOSE: Osteotomy around the knee (OAK) is an established joint-preserving 
procedure. We sought to use large-scale registry data to examine the short-term 
reoperation and adverse outcome rates after OAK.
METHODS: Data on high tibial osteotomy (HTO) and distal femoral osteotomy (DFO) 
patients were extracted from UK National Health Service Hospital Episode 
Statistics (HES). Patients <16 or >80 years and bilateral cases within <6 months 
were excluded. Reoperations and serious complications within 90 days were 
identified using International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision 
(ICD-10) and Office of Population Censuses and Surveys Classification of 
Surgical Operations and Procedures, 4th Revision (OPCS-4) codes. The primary 
outcome was reoperation rate at 90 days and 1 year; secondary outcomes were 
serious medical complications within 90 days, including pulmonary embolism (PE), 
myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI), 
acute kidney injury (AKI), urinary tract infection (UTI) and neurovascular 
injury. Logistic regression was done to estimate odds for serious complications.
RESULTS: A total of 24,947 osteotomies (18,871 HTO, 4490 DFO, 1586 doubles; 
23,371 patients) were included (mean age: 41 years; 62% male; Charlson index 0: 
80.42%). Within 90 days, 2.27% (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.08-2.47) 
underwent a reoperation, including 1.00% (95% CI 0.88-1.13) for infection. At 1 
year, 7.26% (95% CI 6.93-7.61) of patients underwent at least one reoperation, 
including 2.11% for infection (95% CI 1.92-2.30, n = 486); at 1 year, 0.38% (95% 
CI 0.31-0.47) had undergone arthroplasty. Within 90 days, 1.95% (95% CI 
1.78-2.13) experienced at least one adverse event. Specific serious complication 
rates included PE 0.39% (95% CI 0.32-0.47), MI 0.029% (95% CI 0.01-0.05), stroke 
0.029% (95% CI 0.01-0.05) and AKI 0.35% (95% CI 0.28-0.43). Higher comorbidity 
index was consistently associated with higher rates of reoperation and adverse 
events.

young and healthy population, with low 90-day morbidity. Higher comorbidity 
index is the strongest predictor of serious complications. Female patients had a 
lower risk of reoperation but higher adverse event risks. These population-level 
findings will help inform consent discussions and may support future risk 
stratification.

authors: Gillani A, von Eisenhart-Rothe R, Woertler K, Hirschmann MT, Rueckert D, Hinterwimmer F
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4219-4234. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70555. Epub 2026 Aug 3.

Promises and limitations of deep learning for predicting knee osteoarthritis 
progression from medical imaging: A systematic review.

Gillani A(1)(2), von Eisenhart-Rothe R(1), Woertler K(3), Hirschmann MT(4)(5), 
Rueckert D(2)(6), Hinterwimmer F(1)(2).



PURPOSE: To systematically evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and 
translational barriers of deep learning (DL) models for predicting knee 
osteoarthritis (KOA) progression from medical imaging.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of 
Science (inception to June 2026) for peer-reviewed studies applying DL to 
predict KOA progression from medical imaging. Two reviewers independently 
screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using PROBAST-AI. 
The primary outcome was area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 
(AUC). Narrative synthesis was performed due to heterogeneity in imaging 
modalities, outcome definitions, and prediction horizons.
RESULTS: From 1116 records, 33 studies (2019-2026) met the inclusion criteria, 
encompassing 50 predictive models. Sample sizes ranged from 340 to 52,981 knees 
(median: 4298). Nine progression definitions were identified and categorised as 
structural deterioration (n = 14), symptomatic worsening (n = 2), surgical 
endpoints (n = 8) or combined outcomes (n = 9). Nearly all studies (97%) used 
the Osteoarthritis Initiative dataset for training, and only 27% performed 
external validation. Surgery prediction models showed the highest descriptive 
median AUC (0.87), compared with structural (0.78) and symptomatic (0.79) 
progression models, but reflect non-disease factors including access to care. 
MRI-based models showed higher internal median AUCs (0.85) than radiograph-based 
models (0.81), but none underwent external validation. Externally validated 
models showed performance degradation (median AUC: 0.75 vs. 0.81 internal). 
Combining imaging modalities did not consistently improve predictions. However, 
studies leveraging longitudinal trajectories reported higher internal 
performance. Most studies showed low risk of bias in participant selection and 
outcome assessment, but 76% had unclear or high risk in the analysis domain.
CONCLUSIONS: DL models demonstrate proof-of-concept for predicting KOA 
progression but require substantial improvements before clinical deployment. 
Overcoming translational barriers requires standardised progression definitions 
integrating structural and symptomatic outcomes, rigorous multi-site validation, 
and models that effectively leverage multimodal and longitudinal data.

title: Predictive Factors for Manipulations Under Anesthesia After Total Knee Arthroplasty: An Analysis of 15,139 Cases.
authors: Iyer A, Culler M, Telang S, Palmer RC, Jones IA, Lieberman JR, Heckmann ND
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3168-e3177. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-00735. Epub 2026 Jul 23.

Predictive Factors for Manipulations Under Anesthesia After Total Knee 
Arthroplasty: An Analysis of 15,139 Cases.

Iyer A(1), Culler M, Telang S, Palmer RC, Jones IA, Lieberman JR, Heckmann ND.



INTRODUCTION: Limited range of motion (ROM) and arthrofibrosis are complications 
that affect approximately 1 to 13% of patients after primary total knee 
arthroplasty (TKA). Manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) is the preferred 
treatment when failure to achieve adequate ROM in the early postoperative period 
occurs. This study aims to identify predictors for MUA that may guide surgeons 
in preoperative risk stratification.
METHODS: The Premier Healthcare Database was queried to identify patients aged 
18 years or older who underwent elective total knee arthroplasty. Patients who 
underwent manipulation under anesthesia within 90 days of index surgery were 
compared with patients who did not. Demographics, comorbidities, and medication 
usage were compared between cohorts using chi-squared and t-tests. Akaike 
information criterion and Bayesian information criterion minimization was done 
to create an optimal mixed-effects model to identify risk factors.
RESULTS: In total, 975,235 TKAs performed between 2015 and 2021 were identified. 
Of these, 1.55% (15,139) of patients required MUA. Patients in the MUA group 
were younger (62.47 ± 9.19 vs. 67.03 ± 9.24, P < 0.001) and more likely to be 
Black (15.91% vs. 8.29%, P < 0.001). Mixed-effects analysis revealed a decreased 
risk of MUA associated with perioperative dexamethasone (adjusted odds ratio 
[aOR] 0.925, 95% CI, 0.889-0.962, P < 0.001), daily prednisone usage (aOR 0.433, 
95% CI, 0.347-0.542, P < 0.001), and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) 
(aOR 0.882, 95% CI, 0.840-0.927, P < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Younger age, female sex, and Black race were associated with an 
increased risk of MUA after TKA, while perioperative dexamethasone, daily 
steroids, and ARB use were protective. These findings may serve to aid surgeons 
in preoperative risk stratification.

title: Clinical predictors of lateral meniscal hypermobility and development of the Hypermobile Lateral Meniscus Syndrome Score.
authors: Endara Urresta F, Barros Castro A, Peñaherrera-Carrillo C
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 6. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70681.
Online  ahead of print.

Clinical predictors of lateral meniscal hypermobility and development of the 
Hypermobile Lateral Meniscus Syndrome Score.

Endara Urresta F(1), Barros Castro A(2), Peñaherrera-Carrillo C(3).



PURPOSE: To identify independent preoperative predictors of arthroscopically 
confirmed lateral meniscal hypermobility and to develop and internally validate 
the Hypermobile Lateral Meniscus Syndrome Score (HLMSS).
METHODS: A retrospective diagnostic prediction model study included 482 patients 
undergoing knee arthroscopy: 156 with lateral meniscal hypermobility, 171 with 
structural lateral meniscal tears without hypermobility and 155 arthroscopic 
controls. Lateral meniscal hypermobility was defined arthroscopically as 
reproducible anterior translation of the posterior horn beyond the midpoint 
(>50%) of the lateral tibial plateau. Preoperative clinical and magnetic 
resonance imaging (MRI) variables were evaluated as candidate predictors. 
Independent predictors were identified using multivariable logistic regression, 
and the HLMSS was derived from regression coefficients. Internal validation was 
performed using 1000 bootstrap resamples. Discrimination, calibration and 
clinical utility were assessed.
RESULTS: The cohort included 482 patients (mean age, 31.8 ± 9.4 years; 62.4% 
male). Mean age was 28.9 ± 8.1 years in the hypermobility group, 34.7 ± 10.2 
years in the structural tear group, and 31.8 ± 8.7 years in controls; 64.7%, 
60.8% and 61.9% were male, respectively. Independent predictors of lateral 
meniscal hypermobility were intermittent locking (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 
4.78), hyperflexion pain (aOR, 4.21), rotational instability sensation (aOR, 
3.74), posterolateral pain (aOR, 3.12) and popliteomeniscal fascicle abnormality 
on MRI (aOR, 2.68). The HLMSS demonstrated an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.91 
(95% confidence interval [CI], 0.88-0.94) and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.89. 
At ≥7 points, sensitivity was 86.5% and specificity was 84.8%. In the restricted 
comparison with structural lateral meniscal tears, the AUC was 0.84 (95% CI, 
0.80-0.88).
CONCLUSION: The HLMSS demonstrated good to excellent discrimination for 
identifying arthroscopically confirmed lateral meniscal hypermobility using 
preoperative clinical and MRI findings. External validation in consecutive 
symptomatic populations is required before routine clinical implementation.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective diagnostic cohort study.

title: The biplanar cut in medial closing-wedge distal femoral osteotomy is associated with a four-fold lower rate of lateral hinge fractures at non-inferior coronal correction.
authors: Maione A, Pozzi P, Gallizzi S, Parmigiani MD, Romano S, Menon A, Calanna F, Compagnoni R, Ferrua P, Berruto M, Randelli PS
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 6. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70673.
Online  ahead of print.

The biplanar cut in medial closing-wedge distal femoral osteotomy is associated 
with a four-fold lower rate of lateral hinge fractures at non-inferior coronal 
correction.

Maione A(1), Pozzi P(2), Gallizzi S(1)(3), Parmigiani MD(3)(4), Romano S(5), 
Menon A(1)(3)(6), Calanna F(1), Compagnoni R(1)(4)(7), Ferrua P(2)(3), Berruto 
M(8), Randelli PS(1)(3).



PURPOSE: This study compares the outcomes of medial closing-wedge distal femoral 
osteotomy (MCW-DFO) performed with a monoplanar versus a biplanar technique, 
evaluating radiological correction as primary outcome and hinge fracture 
incidence, overall complication profile and patient-reported outcome measures as 
secondary outcomes.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on a consecutive series of 82 
patients (86 knees) with genu valgum who underwent MCW-DFO between 2010 and 
2024. Patients were divided into a monoplanar group (44 knees) and a biplanar 
group (42 knees). Primary outcome was the evaluation of the hip-knee-ankle angle 
(HKA) and lateral distal femoral angle (LDFA), assessed on weight-bearing 
full-length radiographs pre- and postoperatively. Secondary outcomes included 
hinge fracture incidence, overall complication rate and patient-reported outcome 
measures (PROMs) comprising the International Knee Documentation Committee 
score, Knee Society Score, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, Tegner 
Activity Scale and Visual Analogue Scale for pain.
RESULTS: Both groups achieved equivalent and significant coronal correction, 
with no between-group differences in postoperative HKA (180.1° ± 2.5° vs. 
179.8° ± 4.4°, p = 0.502) or LDFA (90.7° ± 2.6° vs. 91.5° ± 4.1°, p = 0.339). 
Hinge fractures were significantly more frequent in the monoplanar group (75.0% 
vs. 19.0%, p < 0.001), and non-inferiority of the biplanar technique was 
formally demonstrated for all radiographic parameters. All PROMs improved 
significantly from baseline in both groups, with the magnitude of improvement 
exceeding the minimal clinically important difference thresholds for all scores.
CONCLUSIONS: Biplanar MCW-DFO protocol was associated with a lower incidence of 
lateral hinge fractures than monoplanar procedure, while achieving comparable 
coronal correction, as formally confirmed by non-inferiority testing. Although 
trends toward better activity level and pain relief were observed in the 
biplanar group, these differences did not retain statistical significance and 
should be considered hypothesis-generating. These findings warrant prospective 
investigation of the biplanar technique as a potentially preferable approach for 
MCW-DFO.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, case-control study.

title: Meniscal and chondral injury patterns in 331 futsal players undergoing anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: Revision cases are associated with increased chondral pathology.
authors: Barastegui D, Ferre-Aniorte A, Velasco P, Vázquez M, Ayestaran I, Alvarez-Diaz P, García-Bordes L, Cugat R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 6. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70675.
Online  ahead of print.

Meniscal and chondral injury patterns in 331 futsal players undergoing anterior 
cruciate ligament reconstruction: Revision cases are associated with increased 
chondral pathology.

Barastegui D(1)(2)(3)(4), Ferre-Aniorte A(1)(3), Velasco P(1)(2), Vázquez 
M(1)(2)(3), Ayestaran I(1)(2)(3), Alvarez-Diaz P(1)(2)(3)(4), García-Bordes 
L(1)(3), Cugat R(1)(2)(3).



PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to characterise the prevalence and 
pattern of associated meniscal and chondral injuries in futsal players 
undergoing anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction, and to identify 
independent predictors of concomitant intra-articular pathology.
METHODS: We retrospectively analysed 331 consecutive futsal players who 
underwent ACL reconstruction at a specialised centre (2020-2024). Review of 
operative reports for ambiguous cases: meniscal tears were classified, excluding 
healed tears, status post-meniscectomy findings and hypermobile menisci without 
structural tears. Multivariate logistic regression models were constructed to 
identify independent predictors of associated injuries.
RESULTS: Mean age was 23.0 ± 5.8 years; 67.7% were male. Injury-to-surgery 
interval was 4.0 ± 3.6 months. Associated injuries were present in 57.1% of 
cases: meniscal tears in 51.4% and chondral lesions in 20.5%. Among 68 patients 
with chondral lesions, Outerbridge Grade 1 was most common (36.8%), followed by 
Grade 2 (42.6%), Grade 3 (13.2%) and Grade 4 (7.4%). Revision cases (10.3%) 
demonstrated markedly higher chondral lesion prevalence (55.9% vs. 16.2%, 
p < 0.001). After multivariate adjustment, revision status was independently 
associated with chondral lesions after adjustment for the included covariates 
(odds ratio [OR] = 6.36, 95% CI = 2.94-13.74; p < 0.001) and combined meniscal 
and chondral pathology (OR = 5.09, 95% CI = 2.25-11.49; p < 0.001). In a 
sensitivity analysis using an Outerbridge Grade ≥ 2 threshold, the association 
was attenuated and did not reach statistical significance (OR = 2.13, 95% 
CI = 0.87-5.23; p = 0.097). Neither sex nor playing surface demonstrated 
independent associations after adjustment.
CONCLUSION: Futsal players undergoing ACL reconstruction present with a high 
prevalence of associated meniscal and chondral lesions. Revision ACL 
reconstruction is associated with substantially higher odds of chondral 
abnormalities, predominantly of low Outerbridge grade. Although the clinical 
significance of these predominantly early cartilage changes requires 
longitudinal confirmation, their presence in a young athletic population 
warrants consideration in surgical planning and patient counselling.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective case series.

title: Clinical outcome of a modern patellofemoral arthroplasty prosthesis into the second decade - a cohort study with minimum 10-year follow-up.
authors: Tsikopoulos K, White P, Musawi HA, Newman J, Porteous A, Robinson J, Murray J, Bristol Knee Group
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Nov 5;64:104664. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104664. Online ahead of 
print.

Clinical outcome of a modern patellofemoral arthroplasty prosthesis into the 
second decade - a cohort study with minimum 10-year follow-up.

Tsikopoulos K(1), White P(2), Musawi HA(3), Newman J(3), Porteous A(4), Robinson 
J(5), Murray J(6); Bristol Knee Group.

Collaborators: Porteous AJ, Robinson JR, Murray JR, Davies DH, Howells N, Clark 
D, Putnis S, Negrut C, Blucher N, Smith JR, Abram S.



BACKGROUND: A modern patello-femoral joint arthroplasty (PFA) prosthesis 
featuring a sided trochlea on-lay component produced in oxinium (i.e., oxidized 
zirconium) has been introduced recently to reduce wear and increase wettability. 
Good medium-term functional outcome and survivorship have been documented as of 
yet. The aim of this study was to explore the long-term outcomes in a 
consecutive series with 10-year follow-up.
METHODS: Data were collected between September 2005 and November 2014 and a 
total of 161 modern PFJ replacements with a mean follow-up of 13.8 years (range 
2 to 22 years) were considered. The primary outcome was the assessment of 
implant survivorship and revisions 10 years post-operatively and beyond. 
Secondary outcomes included the assessment of the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) 
preoperatively, one and five years post-operatively in addition to complications 
and all-cause mortality.
RESULTS: The revision free survival of this modern implant was 92% at 5y, 81% at 
10y, 78% at 15y and 75% at 20 years, and there was no effect for sex 
(P = 0.371), nor age (P = 0.902),nor side (P = 0.554).The mean preoperative and 
five-year postoperative OKSs were 18.83 (SD 7.51) and 30.00 (SD 12.77), 
respectively (mean difference was 11.17 [95% CI 8.17 to 14.17]; P < 0.0001). 
There was a total of 41 revisions, with the most common reason being progression 
of osteoarthritis (n = 24).
CONCLUSIONS: This study shows satisfactory implant survivorship 20 years 
post-operatively and good functional outcomes up to 5 years postoperatively.

title: Kinematic alignment reduces tibial internal rotation and maintains a larger retropatellar contact area than mechanical alignment in early flexion in valgus knees.
authors: Simon JM, Simon F, Siedow TM, Thorwächter C, Traxler H, Bauer L, Holzapfel BM, Müller PE, Niethammer TR, Paulus AC
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70666.
Online  ahead of print.

Kinematic alignment reduces tibial internal rotation and maintains a larger 
retropatellar contact area than mechanical alignment in early flexion in valgus 
knees.

Simon JM(1), Simon F(2), Siedow TM(1), Thorwächter C(1), Traxler H(3), Bauer 
L(4), Holzapfel BM(1), Müller PE(1), Niethammer TR(1), Paulus AC(1)(5).



PURPOSE: Alignment effects after total knee arthroplasty (TKA) may be 
particularly relevant in valgus phenotypes. This study compared kinematic 
alignment (KA) and mechanical alignment (MA) in valgus cadaveric knees during 
active, muscle-loaded flexion, using the native knee as reference.
METHODS: Ten fresh-frozen valgus knees (arithmetic hip-knee-ankle angle [aHKA] 
0.8°-6.4°) were tested in a dynamic knee rig from 30° to 130° of flexion. Each 
specimen was assessed sequentially in its native state and after TKA with KA and 
MA. Tibiofemoral and patellofemoral kinematics were analyzed using 
one-dimensional statistical non-parametric mapping (SnPM1D) with post hoc paired 
F-tests, and retropatellar contact mechanics and quadriceps force using paired 
SPM1D t-tests.
RESULTS: Compared with MA, KA showed less tibial internal rotation during early 
flexion (p = 0.011) and less dynamic valgus deviation in deep flexion 
(p = 0.017), as well as a larger early-flexion retropatellar contact area 
(p < 0.001). Neither condition restored the native anteroposterior translation 
pattern. Patellar tilt differed between KA and MA (p < 0.001); KA showed greater 
internal tilt early in flexion and subsequently shifted toward external tilt. No 
significant differences between KA and MA were detected for patellar shift, peak 
pressure or quadriceps force.
CONCLUSION: Under these experimental conditions, KA and MA produced distinct 
rotational, coronal and patellofemoral responses. Similarity to the native 
reference was outcome- and flexion-dependent. The mild-to-moderate valgus range 
and the simulated muscle loading preclude conclusions about clinical superiority 
or the optimal alignment for valgus TKA.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

title: The presence of cement pockets on the tibial component undersurface is associated with reduced revision for aseptic tibial loosening-A single-centre study of 11,594 total knee arthroplasties.
authors: Firth AM, Remtulla M, Vorasatit L, Nightingale J, Berber R, Matar HE, Van Duren BH, Bloch BV
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70642.
Online  ahead of print.

The presence of cement pockets on the tibial component undersurface is 
associated with reduced revision for aseptic tibial loosening-A single-centre 
study of 11,594 total knee arthroplasties.

Firth AM(1), Remtulla M(1), Vorasatit L(2), Nightingale J(1)(2)(3), Berber R(1), 
Matar HE(1), Van Duren BH(1), Bloch BV(1)(2).



PURPOSE: Aseptic loosening (AL) remains the most common cause of revision 
surgery in primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Numerous mechanisms to explain 
the underlying process of AL have been proposed, with tibial implant design 
thought to influence rates of failure. Tibial baseplates vary in design. The 
incorporation of a recessed area at the implant-cement interface of the tibial 
baseplate, a 'cement pocket', may decrease revision for aseptic tibial loosening 
(ATL). In this study, we assess the effect of such cement pockets on rates of 
revision for ATL across multiple implant designs.
METHODS: We analysed 11,594 consecutive primary cemented total knee 
arthroplasties (TKAs) performed between April 2003 and December 2023 with a 
minimum 2-year follow-up. The use of mobile bearing (MB) or fixed bearing (FB) 
tibial implants and the presence or absence of cement pockets were noted. 
Revisions and the revision indication were identified using our local database 
and the National Joint Registry (NJR). Statistical analysis was undertaken to 
assess the effect of the presence of cement pockets and the tibial articulation 
(FB or MB) on the rates of all-cause revision as well as revision for ATL.
RESULTS: We identified 8591 FB-TKAs; of these, 4753 tibial components 
incorporated cement pocket design and 3838 did not. There were 3003 MB-TKAs, of 
which 942 had cement pockets, and 2061 did not. The presence of cement pockets 
made no significant difference to all-cause revision (ACR) (p = 0.67). Cement 
pockets did significantly reduce the revision rate for ATL for the whole cohort 
(p < 0.01) and for FB-TKAs (p < 0.01) but not for MB-TKAs (p = 0.25).
CONCLUSIONS: The presence of cement pockets appears to reduce the risk of 
revision for AL.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: No significant differences in complication and graft failure rates by type of surgery or osteotomy level after slope-reducing osteotomy with ACL reconstruction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Pineda T, Peña J, Arriagada G, Ugarte J, Olivieri R, Ollivier M
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70665.
Online  ahead of print.

No significant differences in complication and graft failure rates by type of 
surgery or osteotomy level after slope-reducing osteotomy with ACL 
reconstruction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.

Pineda T(1)(2)(3), Peña J(1)(2), Arriagada G(1)(2), Ugarte J(1), Olivieri 
R(1)(2), Ollivier M(4)(5).



PURPOSE: To determine whether anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) graft failure and 
complication rates differ by type of surgery, osteotomy level, or planned 
surgical stages in patients undergoing anterior closing wedge high tibial 
osteotomy combined with ACL reconstruction.
METHODS: A systematic review and meta-analysis searched MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of 
Science, and the Epistemonikos up to September 2026 for studies reporting 
complications in adults undergoing anterior closing wedge high tibial osteotomy 
with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Paired reviewers independently 
screened, extracted, and assessed quality. Random-effects meta-analyses 
estimated overall proportions and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Subgroup 
analyses evaluated differences by type of surgery (primary vs. revision ACL 
reconstruction), osteotomy level (supratubercular, transtubercular or 
infratubercular), and number of planned surgical stages (single- or two-stage 
procedures).
RESULTS: Sixteen observational studies comprising 664 patients (673 knees) were 
included. The estimated graft failure proportion was 1.7% (95% CI: 0.3%-7.9%), 
with no significant differences by type of surgery (p = 0.091), osteotomy level 
(p = 0.770) or planned stages (p = 0.736). Frequent postoperative events 
included symptomatic hardware (7.8%) and complication-related reintervention 
(4.4%). Major complications were uncommon, including delayed union or non-union 
(0.4%), deep infections (0.2%), and vascular or thromboembolic events (0.1%). 
Complication-related reinterventions differed significantly by osteotomy level 
(p = 0.0016), being higher with multiple techniques compared to infratubercular 
and supratubercular approaches. Postoperative recurvatum differed significantly 
by type of surgery (p = 0.0037). The certainty of evidence was rated very low 
for all outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Anterior closing wedge high tibial osteotomy combined with ACL 
reconstruction showed a consistent, low-complication safety profile across type 
of surgery, osteotomy levels, and planned stages, though very low certainty of 
evidence indicates insufficient power to detect differences rather than 
demonstrated equivalence. These findings do not inform optimal treatment 
strategy or timing, and further prospective comparative studies are needed to 
define the incremental benefit of slope correction relative to isolated 
reconstruction.

title: Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.
authors: Jiménez-Martínez J, Gutiérrez-Capote A, Alarcón-López F, Cárdenas-Vélez D
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov 3:3635465261494772. doi: 10.1177/03635465261494772. 
Online ahead of print.

Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL 
Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.

Jiménez-Martínez J(1)(2), Gutiérrez-Capote A(1)(2), Alarcón-López F(3), 
Cárdenas-Vélez D(1)(2).



BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury induces neuroplastic changes 
within the central nervous system (CNS) that may persist beyond reconstruction 
and rehabilitation.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose was to compare neurocognitive performance and 
cortical oscillatory activity between open-skill athletes (eg, soccer, 
basketball, or handball players) without ACL injury history and athletes with 
ACL reconstruction (ACLR) during a probabilistic go/no-go task. It was 
hypothesized that athletes with ACLR would exhibit poorer behavioral performance 
and less efficient oscillatory dynamics, particularly higher theta and lower 
suppression of beta and alpha power oscillations after goal stimulus onset.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 90 open-skill athletes (45 non-ACLR, 45 ACLR) performed a 
probabilistic go/no-go task while electroencephalographic recording was 
performed. Time-frequency analysis targeted midfrontal theta (4-7 Hz), 
left-lateralized central beta (15-25 Hz), and posterior alpha (8-12 Hz) 
oscillations during prestimulus and target stimulus windows. Linear 
mixed-effects models examined group differences in cognitive performance and 
oscillatory power.
RESULTS: Athletes with ACLR showed slower response times and lower accuracy (d = 
0.75-1.09). Midfrontal theta power was attenuated for the ACLR group during the 
prestimulus phase (d = 0.60) yet elevated during target phase trials (d = 0.48), 
indicating a shift from proactive to reactive cognitive control in athletes with 
ACLR. Left-lateralized central beta (d = 0.61) and posterior alpha suppression 
(d = 0.55) were reduced, reflecting impaired motor cortical disinhibition and 
less efficient visual-attentional resource deployment, especially under high 
uncertainty conditions.
CONCLUSION: Athletes with ACLR showed persistent alterations in the cortical 
oscillatory mechanisms associated with conflict monitoring, motor preparation, 
and attentional allocation under uncertainty. These neurocognitive alterations 
may compromise adaptive motor responses in sport contexts characterized by high 
uncertainty and cognitive mental demand, potentially increasing reinjury risk. 
These findings support the integration of neurocognitive assessment into 
return-to-sport protocols.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Alterations in cortical oscillatory dynamics during 
decision-making under uncertainty may reflect reduced efficiency in cognitive 
control, motor preparation, and attentional allocation, which are not detected 
by standard assessments. Exercise professionals should consider integrating 
these assessments into return-to-sport protocols to address the persistent CNS 
alterations that may underlie reinjury risk in athletes with ACLR.

May Have Zone-Specific Effects on the Medial Femoral Condyle and Enhance Repair 
Healing Compared With Isolated Root Repair: An In Vivo Experimental Study in 
Rabbit Knees.

Dzidzishvili L(1), Nelson B(2), Santangelo K(2), Sikes KJ(2), Burton L(2), Del

BACKGROUND: Short-term clinical outcomes of meniscal centralization are 
promising, but questions remain whether it can protect articular cartilage and 
delay osteoarthritis progression.
PURPOSE: To assess cartilage status and healing potential after isolated medial 
meniscus posterior root (MMPR) repair (RR) versus MMPR repair augmented with a 
centralization procedure (RR-CP) in a rabbit stifle model.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: MMPR tears were surgically induced in 16 New Zealand White rabbits. 
Eight underwent RR and 8 underwent RR-CP using interlocking knotless anchors; 
contralateral limbs served as controls. After 4 months, animals were euthanized 
and articular cartilage was harvested for macro- and microscopic evaluation, 
including repair tissue assessment for healing potential. Microscopic assessment 
was performed using the Osteoarthritis Research Society International (OARSI) 
scoring system. Cartilage thickness and meniscal extrusion (ME) were assessed 
using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 9.4 T. The medial 
femoral condyle was divided into 3 regions of interest (anterior, central, and 
posterior), and zone-specific changes were evaluated.
RESULTS: The mean ± standard deviation gross pathology joint degeneration score 
was significantly higher in the RR group compared with the RR-CP group (12.3 ± 
2.2 vs 9.1 ± 2.0; P = .01). The mean OARSI score was significantly lower in the 
RR-CP group compared with the RR group (3.1 ± 1.6 vs 4.2 ± 1.5; P = .04). 
Nonhealed root repairs were more frequent in the RR group, and repair healing 
scores favored the RR-CP group (1.75 ± 0.5 vs 2.5 ± 0.7; P = .041). MRI 
demonstrated significantly reduced central and posterior cartilage thickness in 
the RR group compared with the RR-CP and control knees (P ≤ .02), with no 
difference anteriorly (P = .23). ME did not differ between the RR and RR-CP 
goups (P = .12). Both experimental groups showed greater chondral damage 
compared with contralateral controls (P < .001).
CONCLUSION: RR-CP was associated with reduced total joint cartilage damage and 
improved repair healing compared with isolated RR. MRI showed greater loss of 
central and posterior cartilage thickness after RR, while no difference in 
postoperative ME was detected. Both treatment groups demonstrated increased 
chondral damage compared with control knees.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study provides important biological insights into a 
clinically relevant question and establishes a foundation for future clinical 
investigations aimed at defining patient selection criteria and surgical 
indications for a concomitant meniscal centralization procedure.

title: High-Grade Percutaneous Medial Collateral Ligament Pie-Crusting Is Not Associated With Clinically Meaningful Valgus Instability.
authors: Nishioka T, Thamrongskulsiri N, Casanova F, Ackermann J, Morgan JT, Moews LD, Vega TF, Spaan J, Chahla J
abstract:

Epub  2026 Oct 12.

High-Grade Percutaneous Medial Collateral Ligament Pie-Crusting Is Not 
Associated With Clinically Meaningful Valgus Instability.

Nishioka T(1), Thamrongskulsiri N(2), Casanova F(1), Ackermann J(1), Morgan 
JT(1), Moews LD(1), Vega TF(1), Spaan J(1), Chahla J(1).



BACKGROUND: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) pie-crusting is used during medial 
meniscal surgery to improve visualization and reduce the risk of chondral 
injuries. However, some surgeons extend the release site beyond routine 
incremental perforation, and the effect of this more extensive release on 
postoperative medial laxity remains unclear.
PURPOSE: To determine whether high-grade percutaneous MCL pie-crusting during 
medial meniscus posterior root tear (MMPRT) repair results in clinically 
meaningful valgus instability postoperatively as assessed by valgus stress 
radiography.
STUDY DESIGN: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
METHODS: A retrospective review was performed of patients who underwent isolated 
MMPRT repair with high-grade MCL pie-crusting and no prior knee ligament 
surgery. High-grade pie-crusting was defined intraoperatively by an audible and 
palpable release and a substantial medial compartment opening (≥6 mm) under 
arthroscopic visualization. Postoperative bilateral valgus stress radiographs 
were obtained at a mean of 5.9 ± 2.0 months with the knee positioned at 20° of 
flexion. Gapping was measured in millimeters, and the side-to-side difference 
was calculated using the contralateral knee as an internal control. An a priori 
power analysis based on a 3.2-mm threshold for clinically meaningful 
medial-sided laxity demonstrated a required sample size of 15 patients. The 
side-to-side difference in medial compartment gapping was analyzed using the 
1-sample t test compared with the 3.2-mm threshold.
RESULTS: A total of 21 patients met inclusion criteria. The mean medial 
compartment gapping was 7.84 ± 1.65 mm in the operative knee and 6.62 ± 1.37 mm 
in the contralateral knee. The mean side-to-side difference was 1.21 ± 1.07 mm 
(95% CI, 0.73-1.70 mm). The observed difference was significantly less than the 
3.2-mm threshold associated with clinically meaningful medial-sided instability 
(P < .001).
CONCLUSION: High-grade percutaneous MCL pie-crusting advanced to a defined 
intraoperative endpoint during MMPRT repair resulted in small increases in 
medial compartment gapping that remained below biomechanically defined 
instability thresholds. These preliminary findings suggest that high-grade MCL 
pie-crusting improves visualization and instrumentation without being associated 
with clinically meaningful valgus laxity postoperatively.
