title: Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis Does Not Alter Early Gait Biomechanics After ACL Reconstruction in a Pediatric Population: A Motion Analysis Study.
authors: Manitiu A, Mazy D, Bayol A, Blouin V, Saunders P, Hagemeister N, Nault ML
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov;54(13):3134-3142. doi: 10.1177/03635465261487281.
Epub  2026 Oct 9.

Lateral Extra-articular Tenodesis Does Not Alter Early Gait Biomechanics After 
ACL Reconstruction in a Pediatric Population: A Motion Analysis Study.

Manitiu A(1), Mazy D(1)(2), Bayol A(3), Blouin V(1)(2), Saunders P(1), 
Hagemeister N(3)(4), Nault ML(1)(2).



BACKGROUND: Lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET) is increasingly added to 
anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) to reduce graft failure and 
improve rotatory stability. However, concerns remain that LET may overconstrain 
the lateral compartment, alter gait biomechanics, and contribute to degenerative 
changes, especially in pediatric patients.
HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to compare 3-dimensional (3D) 
knee kinematics during gait between pediatric patients who underwent ACLR with 
LET (ACLR+LET) and those who underwent isolated ACLR (iACLR). It was 
hypothesized that patients with ACLR+LET would show modified postoperative gait 
biomechanics compared to those with iACLR, namely decreased tibial internal 
rotation and increased valgus during the unloading phase.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: This retrospective study included pediatric patients (≤18 years of age) 
who underwent ACLR with or without LET between January 2023 and January 2026. 
All participants underwent standardized gait assessment with knee kinesiography 
pre- and postoperatively. Primary outcomes were 3D knee kinematic waveforms in 
the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes, analyzed using 1-dimensional 
statistical parametric mapping.
RESULTS: In total, 70 pediatric patients (70 knees; mean age 15.8 ± 1.3 years) 
were included: 35 in the iACLR group and 35 in the ACLR+LET group. 
Preoperatively, a small but statistically significant difference in tibial 
rotation (1.8°) was identified between 34% to 38% (P = .032) and 57% to 59% (P = 
.034) of the gait cycle. At approximately 4 months postoperatively (123.3 ± 58.4 
days), no significant between-group differences in knee kinematics were detected 
in any plane of motion (all P > .05). The mean postoperative tibial rotation was 
1.03°± 4.27° in the iACLR group versus 1.61°± 3.51° in the ACLR+LET group.
CONCLUSION: In this pediatric cohort, adding LET to ACLR did not significantly 
alter early 3D gait biomechanics at approximately 4 months postoperatively. 
These findings support the safety of LET as an adjunct to ACLR in young 
patients. Longitudinal studies with higher-demand functional assessments are 
needed to confirm these results beyond the early postoperative period.

Study From the French Arthroscopic Society.

Bouguennec N(1), Neri T(2)(3), Carrozzo A(4), Freychet B(5), Hardy A(6), Herce 
C(1), Kajetanek C(7), Ollivier M(8), Lutz C(9), Cavaignac E(10)(11).



BACKGROUND: Combined anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and medial collateral 
ligament (MCL) injuries are common in pivoting sport athletes and may affect 
postoperative stability and recovery. Although hamstring autografts are widely 
used, concerns persist that harvesting the semitendinosus-gracilis complex could 
impair medial dynamic stabilization in knees with concomitant MCL injury.
HYPOTHESIS/PURPOSE: The purpose was to determine whether MCL status modifies the 
association between ACL graft type and postoperative patient-reported outcomes. 
It was hypothesized that MCL status would not significantly modify this 
relationship.
STUDY DESIGN: Cohort study; Level of evidence, 3.
METHODS: This prospective multicenter registry study included patients 
undergoing primary ACL reconstruction between January 2020 and June 2022 in 
French Arthroscopy Society centers. Patients were categorized by medial injury 
status (isolated ACL, combined ACL-MCL treated nonoperatively, or operatively) 
and graft type (hamstring vs nonhamstring). The primary outcome was the 
International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score. Secondary 
outcomes included Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Return to Sport after Injury 
(ACL-RSI), Subjective Knee Value (SKV), and Tegner activity level. Inverse 
probability weighting based on propensity scores was used to reduce allocation 
bias. Weighted multivariable regression models included graft type, MCL status, 
and a Graft × MCL interaction term.
RESULTS: Of 722 eligible patients, 489 (67.7%) had complete outcome and 
covariate data and were included in the primary analysis. Nonhamstring grafts 
were associated with higher IKDC scores (β = 7.89; 95% CI, 3.45-12.33; P < 
.001). Isolated ACL injuries showed higher IKDC scores than combined ACL-MCL 
injuries treated nonoperatively (β = 10.41; 95% CI, 6.48-14.34; P < .001). The 
Graft × MCL interaction was not statistically significant (operative MCL: β = 
-7.02; 95% CI, -15.26 to 1.22; P = .095), providing no statistically significant 
evidence that MCL status modified the association between graft type and IKDC 
score. Nonhamstring grafts were also associated with higher ACL-RSI (β = 6.15; 
95% CI, 0.02-12.28; P = .049) and SKV (β = 8.87; 95% CI, 4.53-13.21; P < .001), 
whereas no association was observed for Tegner activity level.
CONCLUSION: Nonhamstring grafts were associated with higher patient-reported 
outcome scores overall; however, no statistically significant evidence was found 
that MCL status modified the association between graft type and outcomes after 
ACL reconstruction.

title: A Retensionable Inlay/Onlay Hybrid Double-Bundle Medial Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Produces Superior Restoration of the Uninjured State When Compared to a Single-Bundle Inlay Reconstruction.
authors: Anz AW, Waller G, Carroll J, Colbrunn G, Magoolaghan AC, Truett J, Cohen A, Kulkarni M, Callanan MC
abstract:

A Retensionable Inlay/Onlay Hybrid Double-Bundle Medial Collateral Ligament 
Reconstruction Produces Superior Restoration of the Uninjured State When 
Compared to a Single-Bundle Inlay Reconstruction.

Anz AW(1), Waller G(1), Carroll J(1), Colbrunn G(1)(2), Magoolaghan AC(1)(3), 
Truett J(4), Cohen A(5), Kulkarni M(1), Callanan MC(6).



BACKGROUND: Traditional superficial medial collateral ligament (sMCL) 
reconstruction techniques have not consistently restored native laxity.
PURPOSE/HYPOTHESIS: The purpose of this study was to develop a retensionable 
inlay/onlay hybrid medial collateral ligament (MCL) reconstruction through 
comparison to a biomechanically and clinically validated reconstruction. It was 
hypothesized that increasing the distal footprint on the tibia through a 
double-bundle construct and a retensionable construct would better restore 
native laxity.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 27 cadaveric knees were tested on a 6 degrees of freedom 
robot system. Knees were tested with valgus and external rotation (ER). Each 
knee was tested in a native state and an injured state after sectioning of the 
sMCL. One of 3 reconstructions using an anterior tibialis allograft was then 
performed: (1) single-bundle inlay reconstruction, (2) double-bundle inlay/onlay 
hybrid reconstruction with tibial fixation at both the proximal and distal (PD) 
tibial insertions of the sMCL footprint, or (3) double-bundle inlay/onlay hybrid 
reconstruction with tibial fixation at the anterior and posterior (AP) aspects 
of the distal sMCL tibial insertion. The constructs used retensionable 
variable-loop devices, allowing for retensioning after knee cycling. The 
constructs were tested after cycling and retensioning.
RESULTS: Sectioning of the sMCL resulted in significantly increased laxity 
compared to the native state for both valgus and ER laxity testing (P < .001). 
After flexion cycling and subsequent retensioning, both AP and PD double-bundle 
reconstructions demonstrated significantly higher restoration of stability 
compared to cycled single-bundle reconstructions (P < .001). Both double-bundle 
reconstructions were significantly closer to the native state than the 
single-bundle reconstruction for valgus rotation (P < .001) and ER (P < .05). 
For valgus testing, there was no difference between retensioned double-bundle 
constructs and the native state, with a pooled valgus difference of 0.56° (95% 
CI, 0.05°-1.06°; P = .032). For ER testing, no differences were found between 
the retensioned AP double-bundle and the native state (P = .836), suggesting 
more complete restoration was achieved by AP double-bundle restoration.
CONCLUSION: A retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid double-bundle MCL reconstruction 
with a larger femoral footprint and 2 distal anterior-posterior tibial 
footprints produced superior restoration of the uninjured state when compared to 
a traditional single-bundle inlay reconstruction. For double-bundle 
reconstructions, an anterior-posterior tibial fixation achieved mean values 
closer to the native state than proximal-distal fixation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: A double-bundle retensionable inlay/onlay hybrid 
reconstruction is an effective alternative to a single-bundle inlay 
reconstruction technique. The double-bundle reconstruction may better withstand 
early unrestricted range of motion during postoperative phases.

title: Lateral Tibial Posterior Slope Induces Anterior Tibial Translation While Lateral-Medial Slope Difference Induces Internal Rotation: A Cadaveric Biomechanical Study.
authors: Nejima S, Holt J, van Arkel R, Metcalfe A, Smith N, Amis A
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov;54(13):3171-3180. doi: 10.1177/03635465261480902.
Epub  2026 Sep 22.

Lateral Tibial Posterior Slope Induces Anterior Tibial Translation While 
Lateral-Medial Slope Difference Induces Internal Rotation: A Cadaveric 
Biomechanical Study.

Nejima S(1)(2), Holt J(1), van Arkel R(1), Metcalfe A(3), Smith N(3), Amis A(1).



BACKGROUND: Posterior tibial slope (PTS) influences tibiofemoral kinematics and 
anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) function. While previous studies have evaluated 
symmetrical slope modifications, the isolated influences of the medial or 
lateral PTS remain unclear. This study investigated the influence of medial and 
lateral PTS changes on anterior tibial translation (ATT) and internal rotation 
(IR) under axial loading, using unicondylar slope-changing osteotomies.
HYPOTHESIS: Increased lateral PTS increases ATT, while a greater delta PTS 
(lateral minus medial PTS) increases IR.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen knee specimens were mounted in a custom-built 
fixture in a compression/torsion loading machine. Tibiofemoral 
translation/rotation kinematics were measured under a 500-N axial compression 
load at 0° and 20° of knee flexion using optical motion tracking. Unicondylar 
tibial slope-changing osteotomies were performed on the medial and lateral 
tibial plateaus with a custom cutting guide, preserving key ligament and 
meniscus root attachments. Medial and lateral PTS were independently adjusted to 
-5°, 0°, +5°, and +10°, resulting in medial and lateral PTS ranging from -5° to 
+10°, using 3-dimensionally printed wedges. Repeated-measures analyses of 
variance, post hoc t tests, and Pearson correlations were used for analysis.
RESULTS: An increase of +10° in lateral PTS significantly increased ATT (P = 
.012), while increasing medial PTS did not (P > .99). IR was most influenced by 
delta PTS. At 0° of flexion, altering lateral or medial PTS alone was 
insufficient to significantly change rotation, but changing delta PTS +10° 
produced 7.6° more rotation (P = .015). At 20° of flexion, changing individual 
slopes ±10° significantly increased/decreased rotation (P < .036). The largest 
rotational differences correlated with opposing delta PTS values (r = 0.960; P = 
.0006).
CONCLUSION: Lateral PTS was the principal determinant of ATT, whereas delta PTS 
was the principal determinant of IR under axial loading.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Understanding the independent biomechanical roles of the 
medial and lateral PTS provides insight into mechanisms of anterior and 
rotational instability in ACL injury and reconstruction. These findings suggest 
the potential utility of differential correction of PTS as a novel surgical 
approach for optimizing tibiofemoral rotational kinematics.

title: Youth athlete development and the burden of musculoskeletal injuries: Implications of early sport specialisation.
authors: Maricot A, Tooth C, Nührenbörger C, Seil R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):3871-3877. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70601. Epub 2026 Sep 16.

Youth athlete development and the burden of musculoskeletal injuries: 
Implications of early sport specialisation.

Maricot A(1), Tooth C(1)(2), Nührenbörger C(1)(3), Seil R(1)(2)(4).



Youth sport participation has increased substantially over the past two decades, 
bringing well-documented physical, social and psychological benefits. However, 
this growth has been accompanied by a rising burden of musculoskeletal injuries 
among young athletes, with prevalence rates ranging from 34% to 65%. Overuse 
injuries account for up to 50% of all youth sport injuries, while severe 
injuries such as anterior cruciate ligament reconstructions have increased 
markedly over the past two decades. Early sport specialisation (ESS), defined as 
year-round, intensive, single-sport training that excludes other sports, has 
gained traction as a perceived pathway to elite performance. However, current 
evidence does not support ESS as a reliable predictor of long-term athletic 
success. The majority of successful senior athletes were not standouts as 
youths, and early performance is a poor forecaster of adult excellence. Evidence 
examining associations between ESS and injury risk remains limited and 
methodologically inconsistent. Definitions of ESS vary substantially, 
measurement tools incompletely capture the construct, and relatively few 
high-quality empirical studies are available. More importantly, ESS may be 
better viewed as a proxy for a broader constellation of interacting exposures, 
including cumulative training load, recovery practices, biological maturation, 
variety of movement experiences and psychosocial stressors, which are more 
plausible determinants of injury risk and athlete development. Rather than 
asking whether ESS is inherently harmful, a more informative question is which 
combinations of training, developmental and environmental factors best support 
both performance progression and long-term athlete health. Until these 
mechanisms are more clearly understood, a cautious, individualised and 
evidence-informed approach to youth athlete development is warranted.

title: The Basic Science of Large Language Models in Orthopaedic Surgery.
authors: Dang ABC, Dang ABC
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3012-e3022. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01403. Epub 2026 Aug 5.

The Basic Science of Large Language Models in Orthopaedic Surgery.

Dang ABC(1), Dang ABC.



Orthopaedic surgeons routinely consult search engines, journals, and curated 
websites to stay current on orthopaedic knowledge. The emergence of large 
language models, such as OpenAI ChatGPT and Google MedGemma, is changing the way 
we search for information and how residents learn. Although many orthopaedic 
surgeons are users of artificial intelligence (AI), most are uncertain about how 
these tools actually work and why they sometimes give impressively accurate 
explanations alongside glaring factual errors and fabricated citations. This 
review provides an overview of the underlying preclinical studies behind large 
language models at the level of detail needed to empower orthopaedic surgeons 
with the knowledge needed to critically evaluate AI outputs, design future 
research projects, and effectively incorporate AI tools into clinical practice 
and resident education. Through clinical examples including a Schatzker VI 
tibial plateau fracture and an L4 pedicle screw sizing question, we illustrate 
two distinct classes of AI failure-retrieval failures and reasoning failures-and 
demonstrate how understanding the preclinical studies behind these errors equips 
surgeons to evaluate any AI tool regardless of where or how it runs.

title: Meniscus extrusion assessed by ultrasound does not correlate with knee function or radiographic signs of joint degeneration after medial and lateral meniscus allograft transplantation at a mean follow-up of 13 years.
authors: Wackerle AM, Park YL, Inoue J, Vieider RP, Kamada K, Herman ZJ, Nazzal E, Irrgang JJ, Musahl V, Hughes JD
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 6. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70674.
Online  ahead of print.

Meniscus extrusion assessed by ultrasound does not correlate with knee function 
or radiographic signs of joint degeneration after medial and lateral meniscus 
allograft transplantation at a mean follow-up of 13 years.

Wackerle AM(1)(2), Park YL(3), Inoue J(1)(4), Vieider RP(1)(2), Kamada K(1)(5), 
Herman ZJ(1), Nazzal E(1), Irrgang JJ(1)(6), Musahl V(1), Hughes JD(1)(7).



PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to assess meniscus extrusion using ultrasound 
after meniscus allograft transplantation (MAT) and its association with clinical 
outcomes.
METHODS: Patients who underwent medial or lateral MAT with a minimum 5-year 
follow-up were included. Exclusion criteria included bilateral MAT. Meniscus 
extrusion cross-sectional area (CSA) and extrusion distance, for the index and 
contralateral meniscus, in supine position, bipodal and unipodal stance were 
measured using ultrasound. Joint space width (JSW) and Kellgren and Lawrence 
(KL) grade were assessed on radiographs. The International Knee Documentation 
Committee Subjective Knee Form (IKDC SKF) was collected to assess clinical 
outcomes. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Friedman and analysis of variance 
tests were used to compare meniscus extrusion across weight-bearing conditions. 
Between MAT groups, Mann-Whitney U test and independent-samples t test were 
performed. Multiple regression assessed associations between meniscus extrusion 
and (1) standardized IKDC-SKF, (2) JSW and (3) KL grade.
RESULTS: Thirty-five patients (average age at MAT 29 ± 10 years; 46% females) 
were assessed at a mean follow-up of 13.3 ± 6.7 years. Meniscus extrusion CSA of 
the MAT meniscus, assessed at the latest follow-up, was significantly greater 
than that of the opposite meniscus (supine: 43.2 vs. 20.2; bipodal: 46.2 vs. 
22.7; unipodal: 46.6 vs. 23.8 mm2, p < 0.05). Meniscus extrusion CSA and 
meniscus extrusion distance were significantly greater in the medial MAT group 
compared to the lateral MAT group (p < 0.05). No significant associations were 
found between meniscus extrusion CSA and standardized IKDC SKF, KL grade and JSW 
at final follow-up (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Medial MAT resulted in greater meniscus extrusion than lateral MAT 
in supine position, unipodal and bipodal stance. Meniscus extrusion was not 
significantly associated with clinical outcomes in this cohort and should not be 
considered a surrogate marker for clinical outcomes after MAT; rather, it may be 
better interpreted as a surrogate marker of biomechanical alterations associated 
with the risk of structural joint degeneration.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Proximal Versus Joint Line Medial Collateral Ligament Trephination (Pie-Crusting): Effects on Meniscal Extrusion and Tibiofemoral Contact Mechanics in a Cadaveric Model.
authors: Abbasian M, Partan M, Korabelnikov T, Patel RR, Chen KM, Moteshakereh SM, Zarei H, Arciero RA
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov 5:3635465261485706. doi: 10.1177/03635465261485706. 
Online ahead of print.

Proximal Versus Joint Line Medial Collateral Ligament Trephination 
(Pie-Crusting): Effects on Meniscal Extrusion and Tibiofemoral Contact Mechanics 
in a Cadaveric Model.

Abbasian M(1), Partan M(2), Korabelnikov T(3), Patel RR(3), Chen KM(3), 
Moteshakereh SM(4), Zarei H(4), Arciero RA(2).



BACKGROUND: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) trephination (ie, "pie-crusting") 
is used to improve visualization and working space within the medial compartment 
during knee arthroscopy, but the variability in techniques raises concern for 
meniscotibial ligament injuries, meniscal extrusion (ME), and altered joint 
contact mechanics.
PURPOSE: To evaluate the effects of proximal versus joint line MCL trephination 
on ME and knee contact mechanics.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: A total of 10 fresh-frozen cadaveric knees (5 matched pairs) were 
allocated to 2 groups: proximal trephination and joint line trephination (n = 5 
each). Measurements were obtained in the intact condition and repeated after 
percutaneous MCL trephination. The medial joint opening was assessed 
arthroscopically and radiographically. Under a 1000-N axial load applied for 30 
seconds at 0° and 30° of knee flexion, ME was measured radiographically, and 
tibiofemoral contact pressure and contact area were recorded using an 
intra-articular pressure sensor. All statistical analyses were performed using 
commercial software.
RESULTS: The cadaveric specimens had a mean age of 61.4 years. The joint line 
group required more needle pokes to achieve adequate release. Both techniques 
increased the medial joint opening and ME relative to baseline (all P≤ .05), 
while no significant changes in contact pressure or area were noted. Contact 
pressure was higher after joint line trephination at full extension (P = .018) 
and 30° of flexion (P = .035), although after adjusting for the number of needle 
pokes, a significant difference was only noted at full extension (P = .024). 
Compared with proximal trephination, joint line trephination produced greater 
increases in ME at full extension (P = .026) and 30° of flexion (P < .001) as 
well as a greater decrease in contact area at full extension (P = .021).
CONCLUSION: When comparing joint line and proximal MCL trephination in a 
cadaveric model, both techniques increased the medial joint opening and ME; 
however, joint line trephination caused greater extrusion and less favorable 
contact mechanics than proximal trephination. Further in vivo studies are needed 
to determine the clinical relevance of these findings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This research characterized the biomechanical effects of MCL 
trephination location on ME and joint contact mechanics. This knowledge supports 
favoring proximal trephination to limit iatrogenic disruption of the medial 
compartment.

ai_summary: In a cadaveric model, proximal MCL trephination (pie-crusting) is superior to joint line trephination as it results in less meniscal extrusion and more favorable joint contact mechanics.

title: Knee flexion influences MRI-based static tibiofemoral rotation after ACL injury and reconstruction.
authors: Ackermann J, Jones M, Ball SV, Kabeer AS, Bamania P, Watura C, Lee JC, Williams A
abstract:
1. Knee. 2026 Nov 4;64:104662. doi: 10.1016/j.knee.2026.104662. Online ahead of 
print.

Knee flexion influences MRI-based static tibiofemoral rotation after ACL injury 
and reconstruction.

Ackermann J(1), Jones M(2), Ball SV(2), Kabeer AS(3), Bamania P(3), Watura C(3), 
Lee JC(2), Williams A(2).



PURPOSE: To determine the influence of knee flexion on MRI-based static TF 
rotation, and evaluate whether this relationship is modified by anterior 
cruciate ligament (ACL) state, posterior tibial slope asymmetry (ΔPTS), or 
lateral extra-articular tenodesis (LET).
METHODS: A retrospective review was conducted of professional soccer players who 
underwent primary ACL reconstruction between 2012 and 2024 with available MRI. 
Static TF rotation, medial and lateral PTS, and knee flexion were measured on 
MRI. ΔPTS was defined as the difference between lateral and medial PTS. Linear 
mixed-effects models assessed associations, including interactions for flexion, 
ΔPTS, ACL state, and LET, with adjustment for meniscal status.
RESULTS: A total of 310 MRI examinations from 106 professional soccer players 
(mean age 23.3 ± 4.2 years) with ACL injury (n = 106) and after ACL 
reconstruction (n = 204) were retrospectively analyzed. Greater knee flexion 
during MRI acquisition was associated with increased internal TF rotation 
(β = 0.15° per 1° flexion; 95% CI, 0.02-0.27°; p = 0.020). ΔPTS was a strong 
independent predictor of TF rotation (β = 1.33° per 1° ΔPTS; 95% CI, 0.72-1.95°; 
p < 0.001). A significant flexion × ΔPTS interaction was observed (p = 0.008), 
indicating that the rotational influence of slope asymmetry was greatest near 
extension and diminished at higher flexion angles. A significant ACL 
state × ΔPTS interaction (p = 0.019) demonstrated that the association between 
slope asymmetry and TF rotation was stronger in ACL-deficient knees and 
attenuated after ACL reconstruction. ACL state alone (p = 0.582), LET 
augmentation (p = 0.328), and meniscal variables were not independently 
associated with TF rotation.
CONCLUSION: Knee flexion during MRI acquisition significantly influences axial 
TF rotation. PTS asymmetry remains an independent determinant of rotational 
alignment, although its apparent effect decreases at greater flexion angles and 
after ACL reconstruction. Based on model estimates, a clinically plausible 
10-20° difference in knee flexion during MRI acquisition may produce 
approximately 1.5-3° of apparent static TF rotation. In MRI studies of static TF 
rotation standardizing the flexion angle of knees is critical.

title: Patellofemoral considerations in kinematically aligned total knee arthroplasty: Three-dimensional anatomy and implant-related mismatch.
authors: Malavolta M, Orlandi P, Sassoli I, Sabatini L, Carrozzo A
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70678.
Online  ahead of print.

Patellofemoral considerations in kinematically aligned total knee arthroplasty: 
Three-dimensional anatomy and implant-related mismatch.

Malavolta M(1), Orlandi P(2), Sassoli I(3)(4), Sabatini L(5), Carrozzo A(2)(6).



This Editor's Note considers how three-dimensional trochlear morphology, 
extensor mechanism alignment, patellar reconstruction and implant geometry 
interact in kinematically aligned total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Imaging studies 
suggest that personalised alignment may reproduce selected native trochlear 
parameters more closely than systematic mechanical alignment, although 
rotational and implant-related mismatch persists. Improved anatomical 
reconstruction has not consistently translated into less anterior knee pain or 
better patient-reported outcomes. Native-like trochlear restoration remains a 
plausible biomechanical target, but its clinical benefit has not been 
established consistently across phenotypes and implant designs.

title: The restricted 4D inverse kinematic alignment workflow: A patient-specific approach integrating both bony and laxity phenotypes for total knee arthroplasty planning.
authors: Graichen H, Hirschmann MT, Avram GM, Vandekerckhove PJ, Winnock de Grave P, Indelli PF, Aichmair A, von Eisenhart-Rothe R
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70667.
Online  ahead of print.

The restricted 4D inverse kinematic alignment workflow: A patient-specific 
approach integrating both bony and laxity phenotypes for total knee arthroplasty 
planning.

Graichen H(1), Hirschmann MT(2)(3), Avram GM(2)(4), Vandekerckhove PJ(5), 
Winnock de Grave P(6), Indelli PF(7)(8), Aichmair A(9), von Eisenhart-Rothe 
R(10).



PURPOSE: Two standardized total knee arthroplasty (TKA) balancing goals 
exist-equal gaps or a larger lateral flexion gap. Applying either without 
considering preoperative laxity phenotypes may alter native laxity and 
post-operative kinematics. This study proposes a restricted inverse kinematic 
alignment (iKA)-based technique to integrate bony and laxity phenotypes in three 
dimensions and evaluates its performance using a TKA simulator.
METHODS: The restricted 4D-iKA technique and its boundaries were described and 
validated in 80 knees using the Knee-CAT simulator (MDA). Preoperative MPTA, 
LDFA, HKA and PTS were entered into the simulator and reevaluated after TKA. All 
simulated resections, including posterior condylar offset (PCO), were measured 
in millimetres. The individual laxity phenotype was defined by first recreating 
the bony functional knee phenotype (B-FKP) and then classifying each knee into 
one of nine laxity phenotype types (L-FKP). L-FKP restoration and correction 
were assessed, together with the reconstruction of CPAK and B-FKP types.
RESULTS: Native mMPTA and mLDFA were maintained within the predefined limits in 
varus and neutral knees. In valgus knees, mLDFA was significantly altered 
(MDVAL-LDFA = 2.6° [95% CI = 0.9-4.3°]; p < 0.01), consistent with the 
predefined boundaries. PCO exceeded the predefined ±2 mm reconstruction limit in 
45% of cases, compared to the preoperative state. The predefined target L-FKP IV 
or V was achieved in all cases, except one. In 60% of knees, the lateral flexion 
gap was larger than the medial flexion gap, while in 40% of cases the gaps were 
equal.
CONCLUSION: This first restricted iKA-based technique incorporates 
patient-specific L- and B-FKP to personalize TKA planning. However, balancing 
flexion and extension required increasing PCO by ≥2 mm in 45% of cases. This 
suggests that knee anatomical adjustments should be expected when laxity targets 
are considered.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective, non-comparative study.

title: The Deep Medial Collateral Ligament: Part 2, Structural Properties and Failure Characteristics.
authors: Super JT, Murray IR, Wilebski BJ, Carlson MR, Retzer NK, Tollefson LV, Gaye CE, LaPrade CM, LaPrade RF
abstract:
1. Am J Sports Med. 2026 Nov 3:3635465261497503. doi: 10.1177/03635465261497503. 
Online ahead of print.

The Deep Medial Collateral Ligament: Part 2, Structural Properties and Failure 
Characteristics.

Super JT(1), Murray IR(1), Wilebski BJ(2), Carlson MR(3), Retzer NK(2), 
Tollefson LV(2), Gaye CE(2), LaPrade CM(2), LaPrade RF(2).



BACKGROUND: The deep medial collateral ligament (dMCL) has traditionally been 
described as a capsular thickening deep to the superficial medial collateral 
ligament; however, recent investigations suggest a more extensive anteromedial 
course with a more important role in knee stability. Despite this, its 
structural properties and failure characteristics are not well described.
PURPOSE: To quantify the structural properties of the dMCL, including load to 
failure, stiffness, displacement, and failure location.
STUDY DESIGN: Descriptive laboratory study.
METHODS: Ten fresh-frozen cadaveric knees (mean age, 63.4 ± 4.7 years; range, 
58-70 years; all males; 5 right, 5 left knees; mean body mass index, 26.2 ± 1.9 
kg/m2) were dissected to isolate the dMCL while preserving its meniscofemoral 
and meniscotibial attachments. Specimens were mounted in a 6 degrees of freedom 
robotic system and subjected to preconditioning and then uniaxial 
load-to-failure testing. Load, displacement, stiffness, and failure location 
were recorded.
RESULTS: The mean load to failure of the dMCL was 242.9 ± 86.6 N, with a mean 
stiffness of 25.3 ± 14.3 N/mm and a median displacement at failure of 12.4 mm 
(range, 8.9-31.8 mm). Failure occurred predominantly within the meniscotibial 
portion (9/10 specimens), with only 1 failure in the meniscofemoral portion, and 
none of the specimens failed at the femoral or tibial osseous attachments.
CONCLUSION: When the expanded anteromedial course of the dMCL is included, its 
measured load to failure was higher than values previously reported using more 
restricted anatomic definitions. Failure occurred predominantly within the 
meniscotibial portion. These findings characterize the isolated structural 
properties and predominant failure pattern of the dMCL and may provide reference 
data for future biomechanical evaluation of medial knee reconstruction 
techniques.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Quantification of the structural properties of the dMCL 
provides a biomechanical basis for surgical reconstruction and fixation 
strategies. These data may assist in graft selection and fixation strength 
requirements in anatomic medial knee reconstructions, particularly in patients 
with anteromedial rotatory instability.

title: Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric validation of the Persian version of the University of California, Los Angeles, activity scale in patients following total knee arthroplasty.
authors: Vosoughi F, Nikeghbali G, Koolinia F, Imani M, Entezari A, Menbari Oskouie I
abstract:
1. J ISAKOS. 2026 Nov 5;21:101232. doi: 10.1016/j.jisako.2026.101232. Online
ahead  of print.

Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric validation of the Persian version of 
the University of California, Los Angeles, activity scale in patients following 
total knee arthroplasty.

Vosoughi F(1), Nikeghbali G(2), Koolinia F(3), Imani M(4), Entezari A(5), 
Menbari Oskouie I(6).



INTRODUCTION: The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Activity Scale is 
a widely used score used to assess physical activity. No reliable Persian 
validation of the UCLA score in total knee arthroplasty (TKA) patients exists. 
This study aimed to translate, culturally adapt, and validate the Persian 
version of the UCLA (p-UCLA) activity scale in TKA patients.
METHODS: Following the established cross-cultural guidelines, the UCLA activity 
scale was translated to Persian using forward-backward translation. A total of 
104 TKA patients completed the p-UCLA, Oxford Knee Score (OKS), International 
Knee Documentation Committee Subjective Form (IKDC-SF), and Forgotten Joint 
Score-12 (FJS-12). Construct validity was assessed using the Spearman 
correlation coefficient, while reliability was evaluated using the intraclass 
correlation coefficient (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis. Floor and ceiling 
effects were examined.
RESULTS: The p-UCLA showed excellent test-retest reliability (ICC = 0.98; P < 
0.001). Construct validity was supported by moderate-to-strong correlation with 
OKS (r = 0.75-0.78; P < 0.001), IKDC-SF (r = 0.34-0.66; P < 0.001), and FJS-12 
(r = 0.69; P < 0.001). No floor or ceiling effects were observed. Bland-Altman 
analysis showed minimal bias and high measurement stability.
CONCLUSION: The p-UCLA activity scale is a reliable and valid instrument for 
assessing activity levels in Persian patients after TKA.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Autologous Platelet-Rich Plasma-Enriched Chondral Matrix Implantation Improves Cartilage Repair in an Ovine Model: A Magnetic Resonance Assessment Using the MOCART 2.0 Scoring System.
authors: Peláez P, Damiá Giménez E, Torres-Torrillas M, Hernández-Guerra ÁM, Rubio M, Sopena JJ, Colomer-Selva R, Rodríguez-Altónaga JA, Gonzalo-Orden JM, Vilar Guereño JM, Cugat R, Carrillo JM
abstract:

Autologous Platelet-Rich Plasma-Enriched Chondral Matrix Implantation Improves 
Cartilage Repair in an Ovine Model: A Magnetic Resonance Assessment Using the 
MOCART 2.0 Scoring System.

Peláez P(1)(2), Damiá Giménez E(1)(2), Torres-Torrillas M(1)(2), 
Hernández-Guerra ÁM(1)(2), Rubio M(1)(2), Sopena JJ(1)(2), Colomer-Selva 
R(1)(2), Rodríguez-Altónaga JA(3), Gonzalo-Orden JM(3), Vilar Guereño JM(4), 
Cugat R(2), Carrillo JM(1)(2).



BACKGROUND: Articular cartilage defects exhibit a limited intrinsic regenerative 
capacity and continue to represent a significant challenge in sports medicine, 
frequently progressing to degenerative joint disease if left untreated.
PURPOSE: To assess cartilage repair after autologous chondral platelet-rich 
plasma matrix implantation (PACI) in an ovine model using magnetic resonance 
imaging (MRI) and the MOCART (magnetic resonance observation of cartilage repair 
tissue) 2.0 scoring system.
STUDY DESIGN: Controlled laboratory study.
METHODS: Full-thickness chondral defects (8 mm in diameter) were surgically 
induced in the medial femoral condyles of both stifles in 7 skeletally mature 
Merino sheep (n = 14 stifles). Right stifles were treated with PACI combined 
with intra-articular plasma rich in growth factors (PRGF), whereas left stifles 
received a single intra-articular injection of either Ringer lactate or 
hyaluronic acid. MRI evaluation was performed 18 months postoperatively to 
assess cartilage repair using the MOCART 2.0 knee scoring system.
RESULTS: PACI-treated stifles demonstrated significantly higher MOCART scores 
compared with both control groups. Enhanced defect filling, improved integration 
with adjacent cartilage, and superior repair tissue architecture were observed 
in the PACI group. Furthermore, PACI-treated stifles exhibited signal intensity 
values more closely resembling native cartilage, fewer subchondral alterations, 
and a significantly higher overall MOCART score.
CONCLUSION: PACI combined with PRGF resulted in superior structural cartilage 
repair compared with control treatments in an ovine model, as assessed by MRI. 
These findings support its potential clinical applicability for the management 
of focal cartilage defects in active patients.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This laboratory study demonstrates that PACI combined with 
PRGF improves structural cartilage repair in a clinically relevant ovine model. 
These findings support the potential use of this regenerative approach for the 
treatment of focal articular cartilage defects in active patients.

title: The mechanism of injury's role in jump landing mechanics after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
authors: Hopper HM, Bruce-Leicht AS, Hart JM, Thompson XD
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4201-4209. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70605. Epub 2026 Sep 16.

The mechanism of injury's role in jump landing mechanics after anterior cruciate 
ligament reconstruction.

Hopper HM(1), Bruce-Leicht AS(2), Hart JM(3), Thompson XD(4).



PURPOSE: The primary aim of this study is to determine if there is a difference 
in post-rehabilitation Landing Error Scoring System (LESS) score between 
patients who injured their anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) through a contact or 
noncontact mechanism of injury (MOI). The secondary aim is to determine if there 
is a difference in demographics, strength, and patient-reported outcomes (PROs) 
between patients who injured their ACL through a contact or noncontact MOI.
METHODS: Patients were included from a larger observational laboratory study if 
they had undergone a primary, isolated, uncomplicated ACLR. Patients were 
excluded if they had a history of other lower extremity surgery, concomitant 
ligament injury, surgical complications, or any neurologic disorder.
RESULTS: One hundred and twenty-nine patients were included in this study (age: 
21.4 ± 7.9, sex: 64 F/65 M, follow up: 8.1 ± 1.7 months). Ninety-one patients 
(70.5%) sustained a noncontact MOI, and 38 patients (29.5%) sustained a contact 
MOI. There was no difference in total LESS score (p = 0.930), frontal LESS score 
(p = 0.831) or sagittal LESS score (p = 0.980) between the contact and 
noncontact groups.
CONCLUSION: There was no statistically significant difference in total LESS 
score, frontal LESS score, or sagittal LESS score between contact and noncontact 
MOI. A considerable proportion of participants demonstrated multiple landing 
errors, indicating that assessment and rehabilitation of landing mechanics may 
remain relevant during late-stage rehabilitation. There was no statistically 
significant difference between mechanism of initial ACL injury and strength or 
PROs. The decision to allow a patient to return to play is multifactorial and 
should occur after modifiable risk factors, including jump landing mechanics, 
have been properly mitigated during rehabilitation.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

authors: Jónsdóttir US, Tranberg R, Silbernagel KG, Brorsson A, Briem K
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4187-4194. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70579. Epub 2026 Aug 21.

Effects of fatigue are more pronounced on the uninjured side during single-limb 
jumps 2 years after an acute Achilles tendon rupture.

Jónsdóttir US(1), Tranberg R(1), Silbernagel KG(2), Brorsson A(1), Briem K(3).



PURPOSE: Achilles tendon rupture (ATR) is a serious lower limb injury that may 
result in persistent deficits in strength and endurance of the calf muscles. 
Compensatory mechanisms at proximal joints are known, but the effects of fatigue 
are less studied. The aim was therefore to evaluate the effect of a fatigue 
protocol on lower limb kinetics during performance of single-limb drop 
countermovement jumps (CMJ) in individuals with a history of a unilateral ATR.
METHODS: Thirty participants were recruited on average 2 years after ATR. Drop 
CMJs were performed on each side before and after a fatigue protocol, and peak 
power values for the hip, knee and ankle joints were calculated, as well as jump 
height and duration. A mixed model analysis of variance was used to evaluate 
inter-limb differences pre- and post-fatigue during the landing (eccentric) and 
push-off (concentric) phases of the involved (INV) and uninvolved (UNinv) side.
RESULTS: The fatigue protocol had a greater effect on peak ankle joint power of 
the UNinv side across both phases (by a mean [95% confidence interval, CI] of 
1.06 [0.58-1.54] W/kg) compared to the INV side (0.51 [0.03-1.00] W/kg; 
p = 0.039). Moreover, greater fatigue-induced changes in ankle joint power were 
found during landing (by a mean [95% CI] of 1.13 [0.64-1.61] W/kg) compared to 
push-off (0.45 [0.04-0.93] W/kg; p = 0.011), across both sides. A trend towards 
increased knee joint power was seen as a response to fatigue across both sides 
and phases (p = 0.062), with no change at the hip.
CONCLUSIONS: Rehabilitation following ATR should emphasize progressive reliance 
on the INV side across the rehabilitation continuum by incorporating strength, 
endurance and training under fatigued conditions. This approach may help reduce 
compensatory reliance on the UNinv side, potentially lowering the risk of 
overuse‑related injuries.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception tasks in competitive soccer players.
authors: AminiAghdam S, Woergoetter S, Scharbert J, Baumert P, Fink C
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov 3. doi: 10.1002/ksa.70669.
Online  ahead of print.

Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated 
in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception 
tasks in competitive soccer players.

AminiAghdam S(1)(2)(3)(4), Woergoetter S(3)(4), Scharbert J(3)(4), Baumert 
P(2)(4), Fink C(1)(2)(3)(4)(5).



PURPOSE: This cross-sectional observational study compared jump performance and 
braking-, propulsion- and landing-phase energetics during self-paced 
hands-on-hips single-leg countermovement jump (SL-CMJ) and soccer-relevant 
jump-heading-landing (SR-JHL) between sampled male and female competitive soccer 
players. A secondary aim examined associations between propulsion-phase knee 
positive work (generation) and jump height.
METHODS: Forty-five players (22 males, 18.4 ± 2.1 years; 23 females, 20.1 ± 3.5 
years) performed SL-CMJ and SR-JHL bilaterally using force plates and 
three-dimensional motion capture. SR-JHL incorporated a large-screen interactive 
soccer scene, real-time marker-driven avatar, unrestricted arms, height-scaled 
virtual-ball heading and tested-limb landing. Limb-averaged outcomes included 
jump performance, modified reactive strength index (RSI-mod), phase-specific 
center-of-mass and hip-knee-ankle work and relative joint contribution. Welch 
tests, Hedges' g and false discovery rate (FDR) correction compared sexes within 
tasks; mixed-effects models examined knee energetics-jump height associations.
RESULTS: Males had greater jump height and RSI-mod in both tasks (g = 1.34-2.85; 
q < 0.001), greater propulsion-phase center-of-mass generation and jump 
center-of-mass net work (g = 0.68-1.35; q ≤ 0.033); however, braking or landing 
center-of-mass absorption did not differ significantly between groups after FDR 
correction. Males also showed greater propulsion-phase knee generation, lower 
ankle generation share, higher knee generation share and greater landing knee 
absorption. Absolute propulsion-phase knee generation was associated with jump 
height after accounting for sex and task (β = 0.0147 m per standard deviation; 
p = 0.042), with a stronger association in SR-JHL (p = 0.006).
CONCLUSION: Differences between the sampled male and female cohorts were 
concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation, with greater hip and knee work 
in the male cohort and greater ankle contribution in the female cohort. 
Propulsion-phase knee positive work was associated with jump height, 
particularly in SR-JHL. Because sex was inseparable from cohort context, these 
findings describe between-group differences-not independent sex effects-and 
provide task-specific comparison context for future anterior cruciate ligament 
reconstruction and return-to-sport research.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
authors: Hauer TM, Arner JW, Mauro CS, Bradley JP
abstract:
1. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2026 Nov 1;34(21):e3032-e3040. doi: 
10.5435/JAAOS-D-25-01090. Epub 2026 Aug 6.

Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.

Hauer TM(1), Arner JW, Mauro CS, Bradley JP.



Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from 
sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles 
can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris 
strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a 
dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus 
strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee 
flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and 
ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, 
which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these 
injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% 
muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and 
grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment 
for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but 
reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of 
the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical 
therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. 
Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to 
activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

title: The 2026 ESSKA-ESA formal consensus on partial-thickness posterosuperior rotator cuff tears (Part 1): Definitions, classifications, etiologies, natural history and diagnosis.
authors: Kany J, Iban MAR, Rosso C, Peach C, Métais P, Dias CM, Calvo E, Saccomanno MF, Bøe B, Brilakis E, Bilsel K, Kovacic L, Raebroeckx AV, Gomes N, Martetschläger F, Beaufils P, Dyrna FGE
abstract:
1. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc. 2026 Nov;34(11):4256-4265. doi: 
10.1002/ksa.70587. Epub 2026 Sep 7.

The 2026 ESSKA-ESA formal consensus on partial-thickness posterosuperior rotator 
cuff tears (Part 1): Definitions, classifications, etiologies, natural history 
and diagnosis.

Kany J(1), Iban MAR(2)(3), Rosso C(4)(5), Peach C(6), Métais P(7), Dias CM(8), 
Calvo E(9), Saccomanno MF(10), Bøe B(11), Brilakis E(12), Bilsel K(13), Kovacic 
L(14), Raebroeckx AV(15), Gomes N(16), Martetschläger F(17), Beaufils P(18), 
Dyrna FGE(19).



PURPOSE: To establish evidence-based consensus recommendations regarding the 
diagnosis and treatment of partial-thickness posterosuperior rotator cuff tears 
(PT-PS-RCTs). This part addresses the definition, classification, natural 
history and diagnosis of these controversial conditions in shoulder surgery.
METHODS: This official European Society of Sports Medicine, Knee Surgery and 
Arthroscopy-European Shoulder Associates (ESSKA-ESA) Formal Consensus was 
conducted according to the ESSKA Formal Consensus Methodology. A Steering Group 
developed 33 questions, followed by a standardized literature search and 
evidence review. For each question, a consensus statement was drafted and 
assigned recommendation grades (A-D) according to the level of evidence. An 
independent Rating Group evaluated all statements until strong agreement was 
achieved.
RESULTS: Twelve recommendations were generated with three Grade A, three Grade 
B, two Grade C, five Grade D and strong agreement. Grade A was found for the use 
of multiple classification systems in unison to characterize these injuries and 
for the distinction between acute and chronic tears. Scientific presumption 
level (Grade B) was found for the increased incidence of articular injuries in 
overhead and contact athletes and for the absence of a link between calcifying 
tendinitis and PT-PS-RCTs. Grade C was found to define the risk and timeframe of 
tear progression and the ideal imaging modality.
CONCLUSION: This ESSKA-ESA Formal Consensus recommends that PT-PS-RCTs should be 
classified according to tear location, depth and tendon involvement. The 
aetiology of these injuries is multifactorial, and their progression is 
unpredictable. Current imaging modalities have limitations in characterizing 
these lesions. The present consensus provides clinicians with a practical 
evidence-based framework for the diagnosis and classification of PT-PS-RCTs 
while identifying key priorities for future clinical research.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I formal consensus.
